{{Short description|Graph representation in quantum mechanics}}
[[File:Tensor contraction diagram.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|Graphical notation for the contraction <math>C_{ik}=\sum_j A_{ij}B_{jk}</math>: vertices denote tensors, an edge joining two vertices denotes the summed index <math>j</math>, and the open edges denote the free indices <math>i</math> and <math>k</math>.]]
[[File:MPS diagram.svg|thumb|upright=1.6|Diagrammatic representation of a matrix product state on twelve sites: every circle is a tensor ''A'' carrying one physical index (vertical leg, dimension ''d'') and two virtual indices (horizontal legs, bond dimension ''D'') that are contracted with the neighbouring tensors. The bond dimension controls the amount of entanglement the state can carry.]]
A '''tensor network''' is a representation of a high-dimensional array or [[multilinear map]] as a collection of smaller [[tensor]]s whose indices are contracted according to a graph: vertices represent tensors, an edge joining two vertices represents an index that is summed over, and an open edge represents a free index of the resulting object; the dimension of an internal edge is called its ''bond dimension''.<ref name="bridgeman">{{cite journal |last1=Bridgeman |first1=J. C. |last2=Chubb |first2=C. T. |title=Hand-waving and interpretive dance: an introductory course on tensor networks |journal=Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and Theoretical |volume=50 |issue=22 |pages=223001 |year=2017 |doi=10.1088/1751-8121/aa6dc3 |arxiv=1603.03039 |bibcode=2017JPhA...50v3001B }}</ref> Tensor networks can represent many-body wave functions and density operators, partition functions, Hamiltonians and other linear maps, probability distributions, and quantum circuits.

The usefulness of a tensor network representation rests on two pillars: compression and contraction. When the required bond dimensions remain moderate and the graph admits a favourable contraction order, the storage and computational costs can be exponentially smaller than for the explicit high-dimensional object. Neither condition holds in general — the required bond dimensions can grow rapidly, and the exact contraction of a general network is computationally intractable<ref name="markov-shi" /> — so the power of the formalism lies in identifying the structured problems for which compression and contraction are both efficient.

'''Tensor network states''' are the special case in which a tensor network represents a variational wave function of a quantum many-body system — one of the principal settings in which the formalism was developed. The best-known examples are [[matrix product state]]s (MPS) in one dimension, projected entangled pair states (PEPS) in two and higher dimensions, tree tensor networks (TTN), and the multiscale entanglement renormalization ansatz (MERA). Tensor networks provide the theoretical and computational framework underlying the [[density matrix renormalization group]] (DMRG), which effectively turned the simulation of quantum spin chains from a problem of exponential complexity into one of polynomial complexity, and remains widely used for simulating strongly correlated quantum systems.<ref name="rmp">{{cite journal |last1=Cirac |first1=J. I. |last2=Pérez-García |first2=D. |last3=Schuch |first3=N. |last4=Verstraete |first4=F. |title=Matrix product states and projected entangled pair states: Concepts, symmetries, theorems |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |volume=93 |article-number=045003 |year=2021 |issue=4 |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.93.045003 |arxiv=2011.12127 |bibcode=2021RvMP...93d5003C }}</ref><ref name="dmrg30">{{cite journal |last1=Verstraete |first1=F. |last2=Nishino |first2=T. |last3=Schollwöck |first3=U. |last4=Bañuls |first4=M. C. |last5=Chan |first5=G. K. |last6=Stoudenmire |first6=E. M. |title=Density matrix renormalization group, 30 years on |journal=Nature Reviews Physics |volume=5 |pages=273–276 |year=2023 |issue=5 |doi=10.1038/s42254-023-00572-5 |bibcode=2023NatRP...5..273V }}</ref>

A central idea behind tensor-network methods is that many physically relevant low-energy states of local quantum Hamiltonians occupy a comparatively small, weakly entangled part of the exponentially large many-body [[Hilbert space]]; in important settings their entanglement obeys an [[Entanglement entropy#Area law|area law]].<ref name="hastings" /><ref name="eisert" /> Tensor network states are designed to efficiently parameterize such states: the entanglement between different regions is routed through auxiliary "virtual" indices whose dimension (the ''bond dimension'') controls the amount of entanglement the ansatz can accommodate, and which serves as a systematically improvable refinement parameter.<ref name="rmp" /> A second defining feature of the formalism is its diagrammatic calculus, descending from the graphical notation introduced by [[Roger Penrose]], in which multilinear-algebraic manipulations are performed by deforming pictures of the network.<ref name="penrose" />

Beyond condensed matter physics, tensor networks are used in numerical multilinear algebra and scientific computing, fluid dynamics, quantum chemistry, quantum field theory and lattice gauge theory, classical statistical mechanics, probabilistic inference, quantum error correction, machine learning, and the classical simulation of quantum computers. In computational fluid dynamics, tensor-train and matrix-product-state representations have been used to compress and simulate turbulent flows and to represent high-dimensional turbulence probability distributions.<ref name="gourianov-turbulence">{{cite journal |last1=Gourianov |first1=N. |last2=Lubasch |first2=M. |last3=Dolgov |first3=S. |last4=van den Berg |first4=Q. Y. |last5=Babaee |first5=H. |last6=Givi |first6=P. |last7=Kiffner |first7=M. |last8=Jaksch |first8=D. |title=A quantum-inspired approach to exploit turbulence structures |journal=Nature Computational Science |volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=30–37 |year=2022 |doi=10.1038/s43588-021-00181-1 |pmid=38177703 |arxiv=2106.05782}}</ref><ref name="gourianov-pdf">{{cite journal |last1=Gourianov |first1=N. |last2=Givi |first2=P. |last3=Jaksch |first3=D. |last4=Pope |first4=S. B. |title=Tensor networks enable the calculation of turbulence probability distributions |journal=Science Advances |volume=11 |issue=5 |article-number=eads5990 |year=2025 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.ads5990 |pmid=39879287 |pmc=13109950 |arxiv=2407.09169 |bibcode=2025SciA...11S5990G }}</ref> In numerical analysis, tensor cross interpolation (TCI) constructs low-rank tensor-train or matrix-product-state representations by adaptively sampling selected entries of a high-dimensional tensor, with applications including multidimensional integration, partial differential equations, partition functions and matrix product operators.<ref name="tci">{{cite journal |last1=Núñez Fernández |first1=Y. |last2=Ritter |first2=M. K. |last3=Jeannin |first3=M. |last4=Li |first4=J.-W. |last5=Kloss |first5=T. |last6=Louvet |first6=T. |last7=Terasaki |first7=S. |last8=Parcollet |first8=O. |last9=von Delft |first9=J. |last10=Shinaoka |first10=H. |last11=Waintal |first11=X. |title=Learning tensor networks with tensor cross interpolation: New algorithms and libraries |journal=SciPost Physics |volume=18 |article-number=104 |year=2025 |issue=3 |doi=10.21468/SciPostPhys.18.3.104  |doi-access=free|arxiv=2407.02454 |bibcode=2025ScPP...18..104N }}</ref> Tensor network contraction techniques have also been used to reproduce — and in several cases surpass — the results of leading [[quantum supremacy]] experiments on classical hardware.<ref name="pan-sampling" /><ref name="liu-sc21" /><ref name="tindall-ibm" />

== General ideas ==
The Hilbert space of a quantum many-body system grows exponentially with the number of its constituents: a lattice of <math>N</math> spin-1/2 particles requires <math>2^N</math> complex amplitudes for a complete description. A generic state in this space exhibits near-maximal entanglement between any subsystem and its complement. Ground states of local Hamiltonians are, however, far from generic. For gapped one-dimensional systems it has been proven that the entanglement entropy of a contiguous block saturates — an ''area law'' — rather than growing with the block size,<ref name="hastings">{{cite journal |last1=Hastings |first1=M. B. |title=An area law for one-dimensional quantum systems |journal=Journal of Statistical Mechanics: Theory and Experiment |volume=2007 |pages=08024 |year=2007 |issue=8 |doi=10.1088/1742-5468/2007/08/P08024 |arxiv=0705.2024 |bibcode=2007JSMTE..08...24H }}</ref> and any state whose [[Rényi entropy|Rényi entanglement entropies]] scale at most logarithmically can be represented ''faithfully'' and efficiently as a matrix product state, with an error that can be controlled polynomially in the bond dimension.<ref name="faithfully">{{cite journal |last1=Verstraete |first1=F. |last2=Cirac |first2=J. I. |title=Matrix product states represent ground states faithfully |journal=Physical Review B |volume=73 |article-number=094423 |year=2006 |issue=9 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.73.094423 |arxiv=cond-mat/0505140 |bibcode=2006PhRvB..73i4423V }}</ref> The precise conditions on entropy scaling under which such efficient approximability holds or fails have been delineated in detail.<ref name="schuch-entropy">{{cite journal |last1=Schuch |first1=N. |last2=Wolf |first2=M. M. |last3=Verstraete |first3=F. |last4=Cirac |first4=J. I. |title=Entropy scaling and simulability by matrix product states |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=100 |article-number=030504 |year=2008 |issue=3 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.100.030504 |pmid=18232955 |arxiv=0705.0292 |bibcode=2008PhRvL.100c0504S }}</ref> The idea that physical states occupy only a tiny corner of Hilbert space was made precise using tools of quantum information theory: the overwhelming majority of Hilbert space is physically inaccessible, and the full Hilbert space is in this sense a "convenient illusion".<ref name="poulin">{{cite journal |last1=Poulin |first1=D. |last2=Qarry |first2=A. |last3=Somma |first3=R. |last4=Verstraete |first4=F. |title=Quantum simulation of time-dependent Hamiltonians and the convenient illusion of Hilbert space |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=106 |article-number=170501 |year=2011 |issue=17 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.106.170501 |pmid=21635023 |arxiv=1102.1360 |bibcode=2011PhRvL.106q0501P }}</ref> The program of constructing variational classes of states that parameterize precisely the physical, low-entanglement corner of Hilbert space — with the entanglement structure built in from the outset — was formulated in the original projected entangled pair states paper.<ref name="peps">{{cite arXiv |last1=Verstraete |first1=F. |last2=Cirac |first2=J. I. |title=Renormalization algorithms for quantum-many body systems in two and higher dimensions |year=2004 |eprint=cond-mat/0407066 }}</ref> By construction, the entanglement entropy of a region in an MPS or PEPS is bounded by the virtual bonds crossing its boundary, so these ansätze satisfy corresponding area-law bounds automatically.<ref name="rmp" />

The same considerations apply to the classical simulation of quantum circuits. Quantum circuits that generate limited amounts of entanglement — or whose geometry permits efficient contraction — can be simulated classically using tensor network methods, and those have become the standard tool for probing the claims of [[quantum supremacy]] experiments. Tensor network contraction algorithms have indeed been used to solve the sampling problem of Google's Sycamore random-circuit experiment on classical hardware,<ref name="pan-bigbatch">{{cite journal |last1=Pan |first1=F. |last2=Zhang |first2=P. |title=Simulation of quantum circuits using the big-batch tensor network method |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=128 |article-number=030501 |year=2022 |issue=3 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.128.030501 |pmid=35119890 |arxiv=2103.03074 |bibcode=2022PhRvL.128c0501P }}</ref><ref name="pan-sampling">{{cite journal |last1=Pan |first1=F. |last2=Chen |first2=K. |last3=Zhang |first3=P. |title=Solving the sampling problem of the Sycamore quantum circuits |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=129 |article-number=090502 |year=2022 |issue=9 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.129.090502 |pmid=36083655 |arxiv=2111.03011 |bibcode=2022PhRvL.129i0502P }}</ref> to perform a real-time simulation of the same circuits on the Sunway supercomputer (awarded the 2021 [[Gordon Bell Prize]]),<ref name="liu-sc21">{{cite conference |last1=Liu |first1=Y. |last2=Liu |first2=X. |last3=Li |first3=F. |last4=Fu |first4=H. |last5=Yang |first5=Y. |last6=Song |first6=J. |last7=Zhao |first7=P. |last8=Wang |first8=Z. |last9=Peng |first9=D. |last10=Chen |first10=H. |last11=Guo |first11=C. |last12=Huang |first12=H. |last13=Wu |first13=W. |last14=Chen |first14=D. |title=Closing the "quantum supremacy" gap: achieving real-time simulation of a random quantum circuit using a new Sunway supercomputer |conference=Proceedings of the International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis (SC '21) |pages=1–12 |year=2021 |doi=10.1145/3458817.3487399 |arxiv=2110.14502}}</ref> and to reproduce and surpass, on modest classical resources, the results of IBM's 127-qubit "quantum utility" experiment.<ref name="tindall-ibm">{{cite journal |last1=Tindall |first1=J. |last2=Fishman |first2=M. |last3=Stoudenmire |first3=E. M. |last4=Sels |first4=D. |title=Efficient tensor network simulation of IBM's Eagle kicked Ising experiment |journal=PRX Quantum |volume=5 |article-number=010308 |year=2024 |issue=1 |doi=10.1103/PRXQuantum.5.010308 |arxiv=2306.14887 |bibcode=2024PRXQ....5a0308T }}</ref><ref name="begusic">{{cite journal |last1=Begušić |first1=T. |last2=Gray |first2=J. |last3=Chan |first3=G. K.-L. |title=Fast and converged classical simulations of evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance |journal=Science Advances |volume=10 |article-number=eadk4321 |year=2024 |issue=3 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.adk4321 |pmid=38232163 |pmc=12697566 |arxiv=2308.05077 |bibcode=2024SciA...10K4321B }}</ref>

== Graphical calculus ==
Tensor networks are almost universally manipulated in a diagrammatic notation that goes back to Penrose: a tensor is drawn as a shape with one leg per index, and the contraction of two indices is drawn by joining the corresponding legs.<ref name="penrose">{{cite book |last1=Penrose |first1=R. |chapter=Applications of negative dimensional tensors |title=Combinatorial Mathematics and its Applications |editor=D. J. A. Welsh |publisher=Academic Press |year=1971 |pages=221–244}}</ref> A matrix product state is then a chain of three-legged tensors, a PEPS a grid of five-legged tensors, an expectation value a closed ("fully contracted") diagram, and so on. Much of the power of the formalism resides in this graphical calculus: identities of multilinear algebra that would be opaque as nested index sums become topological deformations of a picture, and many key theorems — gauge freedom, canonical forms, transfer matrix manipulations, the behaviour of symmetries — are most naturally stated and proved diagrammatically.<ref name="rmp" /> The same diagrams describe quantum circuits, quantum channels, and partition functions of classical statistical models, which is what allows concepts and algorithms to be transferred so easily among these settings.

A closely related but historically later development in quantum information theory is the [[ZX-calculus]], a complete graphical rewrite system for qubit tensor networks generated by so-called Z- and X-spiders.<ref name="zx">{{cite journal |last1=Coecke |first1=B. |last2=Duncan |first2=R. |title=Interacting quantum observables: categorical algebra and diagrammatics |journal=New Journal of Physics |volume=13 |article-number=043016 |year=2011 |issue=4 |doi=10.1088/1367-2630/13/4/043016 |arxiv=0906.4725 |bibcode=2011NJPh...13d3016C }}</ref> The ZX-calculus can be regarded as a highly simplified species of tensor network, specialized to qubits and generated by a small set of spider tensors with phase parameters; within this restricted setting the diagrammatic rewrite rules can be made ''complete'' — complete axiomatisations are known for universal pure-qubit quantum mechanics as well as for important restricted fragments<ref name="zx-complete">{{cite journal |last1=Jeandel |first1=E. |last2=Perdrix |first2=S. |last3=Vilmart |first3=R. |title=Completeness of the ZX-calculus |journal=Logical Methods in Computer Science |volume=16 |issue=2 |pages=11 |year=2020 |doi=10.23638/LMCS-16(2:11)2020 |doi-access=free |arxiv=1903.06035}}</ref> — and it is widely used for quantum circuit verification, optimization and fault-tolerance constructions.<ref name="zx-opt">{{cite journal |last1=Duncan |first1=R. |last2=Kissinger |first2=A. |last3=Perdrix |first3=S. |last4=van de Wetering |first4=J. |title=Graph-theoretic simplification of quantum circuits with the ZX-calculus |journal=Quantum |volume=4 |article-number=279 |year=2020 |doi=10.22331/q-2020-06-04-279 |doi-access=free |arxiv=1902.03178 |bibcode=2020Quant...4..279D }}</ref>
== Common network geometries ==
The same graphical rules apply to many network topologies; the names in the following table distinguish the most common geometries and choices of open indices.<ref name="rmp" /><ref name="cichocki">{{cite journal |last1=Cichocki |first1=A. |last2=Lee |first2=N. |last3=Oseledets |first3=I. V. |last4=Phan |first4=A.-H. |last5=Zhao |first5=Q. |last6=Mandic |first6=D. P. |title=Tensor networks for dimensionality reduction and large-scale optimization: Part 1, low-rank tensor decompositions |journal=Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning |volume=9 |issue=4–5 |pages=249–429 |year=2016 |doi=10.1561/2200000059 |arxiv=1609.00893}}</ref> The geometries differ not only in expressive power but also in contraction cost: chains and trees admit efficient exact contraction at fixed bond dimension, whereas networks containing large loops generally require approximate contraction.

! Form

|-
| [[Matrix product state]] (MPS) / tensor train (TT)
| A chain of tensors, of rank three in the interior, with the physical or data indices left open
| One-dimensional quantum states; compression of high-order arrays
|-
| Matrix product operator (MPO) / tensor-train operator
| A chain with one input and one output index at each site
| Hamiltonians, transfer matrices, density operators, channels
|-
| Tree tensor network (TTN)
| A loop-free hierarchy of tensors combining the branches of a tree; closely related to the hierarchical Tucker format
| Hierarchical correlations, multiscale approximation, high-dimensional numerical problems

| Higher-dimensional quantum states; classical partition functions
|-

| A layered network of isometries and disentanglers with a causal-cone structure
| Critical systems; real-space renormalization
|-

| A continuum limit of the MPS construction
| One-dimensional quantum fields

== History ==

=== Statistical mechanics origins ===
The prehistory of tensor networks lies in classical statistical mechanics. In 1941 [[Hendrik Kramers|Kramers]] and [[Gregory Wannier|Wannier]] introduced the [[transfer matrix]] treatment of the two-dimensional [[Ising model]] together with a variational method for its leading eigenvector, based on a class of trial states that are recognizable in hindsight as precursors of matrix product states.<ref name="kramers-wannier">{{cite journal |last1=Kramers |first1=H. A. |last2=Wannier |first2=G. H. |title=Statistics of the two-dimensional ferromagnet. Part I |journal=Physical Review |volume=60 |pages=252–262 |year=1941 |issue=3 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.60.252 |bibcode=1941PhRv...60..252K }}</ref><ref name="kramers-wannier2">{{cite journal |last1=Kramers |first1=H. A. |last2=Wannier |first2=G. H. |title=Statistics of the two-dimensional ferromagnet. Part II |journal=Physical Review |volume=60 |pages=263–276 |year=1941 |issue=3 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.60.263 |bibcode=1941PhRv...60..263K }}</ref> In the language of the modern field, their transfer matrices are matrix product operators and their variational ansatz an MPS with a bond dimension equal to the physical dimension. [[Rodney Baxter|Baxter]] developed these ideas much further, introducing the [[corner transfer matrix]] formalism and using matrix-product-like variational calculations to compute thermodynamic quantities of classical lattice models to high precision.<ref name="baxter1968">{{cite journal |last1=Baxter |first1=R. J. |title=Dimers on a rectangular lattice |journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics |volume=9 |pages=650–654 |year=1968 |issue=4 |doi=10.1063/1.1664623 |bibcode=1968JMP.....9..650B }}</ref><ref name="baxter1978">{{cite journal |last1=Baxter |first1=R. J. |title=Variational approximations for square lattice models in statistical mechanics |journal=Journal of Statistical Physics |volume=19 |pages=461–478 |year=1978 |issue=5 |doi=10.1007/BF01011693 |bibcode=1978JSP....19..461B }}</ref>

This variational transfer-matrix tradition was carried on through the 1970s: Kelland applied it to the Potts model,<ref name="kelland">{{cite journal |last1=Kelland |first1=S. B. |title=Estimates of the critical exponent β for the Potts model using a variational approximation |journal=Canadian Journal of Physics |volume=54 |pages=1621–1626 |year=1976 |issue=15 |doi=10.1139/p76-191 |bibcode=1976CaJPh..54.1621K }}</ref> Tsang studied square-lattice variational approximations to the Ising model,<ref name="tsang">{{cite journal |last1=Tsang |first1=S. K. |title=Square lattice variational approximations applied to the Ising model |journal=Journal of Statistical Physics |volume=20 |pages=95–114 |year=1979 |issue=1 |doi=10.1007/BF01013748 |bibcode=1979JSP....20...95T }}</ref> and Baxter and Enting used corner transfer matrices to generate efficient series expansions;<ref name="baxter-enting">{{cite journal |last1=Baxter |first1=R. J. |last2=Enting |first2=I. G. |title=Series expansions from corner transfer matrices: The square lattice Ising model |journal=Journal of Statistical Physics |volume=21 |pages=103–123 |year=1979 |issue=2 |doi=10.1007/BF01008694 |bibcode=1979JSP....21..103B }}</ref> the corner transfer matrix formalism is treated in Baxter's classic monograph.<ref name="baxter-book">{{cite book |last1=Baxter |first1=R. J. |title=Exactly Solved Models in Statistical Mechanics |publisher=Academic Press |year=1982 |isbn=978-0-12-083180-7}}</ref> Nightingale and Blöte generalized Baxter's variational method to quantum Hamiltonians, using a matrix-product-type trial state as the guiding function of a Monte Carlo computation of the Haldane gap of the spin-1 Heisenberg chain.<ref name="nightingale">{{cite journal |last1=Nightingale |first1=M. P. |last2=Blöte |first2=H. W. J. |title=Gap of the linear spin-1 Heisenberg antiferromagnet: A Monte Carlo calculation |journal=Physical Review B |volume=33 |pages=659–661 |year=1986 |issue=1 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.33.659 |pmid=9937971 |bibcode=1986PhRvB..33..659N |url=https://digitalcommons.uri.edu/phys_facpubs/241 }}</ref>

A separate thread originated with [[Kenneth G. Wilson|Wilson's]] [[numerical renormalization group]] (NRG), devised in the 1970s to solve the [[Kondo problem]].<ref name="wilson">{{cite journal |last1=Wilson |first1=K. G. |title=The renormalization group: Critical phenomena and the Kondo problem |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |volume=47 |pages=773–840 |year=1975 |issue=4 |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.47.773 |bibcode=1975RvMP...47..773W }}</ref> It was understood only three decades later that NRG is itself a variational method within the class of matrix product states, which allowed its systematic improvement and unification with DMRG.<ref name="weichselbaum">{{cite journal |last1=Weichselbaum |first1=A. |last2=Verstraete |first2=F. |last3=Schollwöck |first3=U. |last4=Cirac |first4=J. I. |last5=von Delft |first5=J. |title=Variational matrix-product-state approach to quantum impurity models |journal=Physical Review B |volume=80 |article-number=165117 |year=2009 |issue=16 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.80.165117 |arxiv=cond-mat/0504305 |bibcode=2009PhRvB..80p5117W }}</ref>

=== Matrix product states in mathematical physics ===
On the quantum side, Accardi introduced states of matrix product form in the early 1980s in his study of quantum [[Markov chain]]s.<ref name="accardi">{{cite journal |last1=Accardi |first1=L. |title=Topics in quantum probability |journal=Physics Reports |volume=77 |pages=169–192 |year=1981 |issue=3 |doi=10.1016/0370-1573(81)90070-3 |bibcode=1981PhR....77..169A |hdl=2108/82347 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> The most famous matrix product state was written down by [[AKLT model|Affleck, Kennedy, Lieb and Tasaki]] (AKLT) in 1987, as a rigorous example supporting the [[Haldane conjecture]] for integer-spin Heisenberg chains; the same authors also constructed two-dimensional analogues that are now recognized as PEPS.<ref name="aklt-prl">{{cite journal |last1=Affleck |first1=I. |last2=Kennedy |first2=T. |last3=Lieb |first3=E. H. |last4=Tasaki |first4=H. |title=Rigorous results on valence-bond ground states in antiferromagnets |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=59 |pages=799–802 |year=1987 |issue=7 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.59.799 |pmid=10035874 |bibcode=1987PhRvL..59..799A }}</ref><ref name="aklt-cmp">{{cite journal |last1=Affleck |first1=I. |last2=Kennedy |first2=T. |last3=Lieb |first3=E. H. |last4=Tasaki |first4=H. |title=Valence bond ground states in isotropic quantum antiferromagnets |journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics |volume=115 |pages=477–528 |year=1988 |issue=3 |doi=10.1007/BF01218021 |bibcode=1988CMaPh.115..477A }}</ref> Fannes, Nachtergaele and Werner realized that the AKLT state is one member of a vastly larger class, which they called ''finitely correlated states'' — injective matrix product states in modern terminology — and in a series of papers between 1989 and 1992 they developed the rigorous theory of these states, proving in particular that they arise as unique gapped ground states of local parent Hamiltonians.<ref name="fnw-epl">{{cite journal |last1=Fannes |first1=M. |last2=Nachtergaele |first2=B. |last3=Werner |first3=R. F. |title=Exact antiferromagnetic ground states of quantum spin chains |journal=Europhysics Letters |volume=10 |pages=633–637 |year=1989 |issue=7 |doi=10.1209/0295-5075/10/7/005 |bibcode=1989EL.....10..633F }}</ref><ref name="fnw-cmp">{{cite journal |last1=Fannes |first1=M. |last2=Nachtergaele |first2=B. |last3=Werner |first3=R. F. |title=Finitely correlated states on quantum spin chains |journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics |volume=144 |pages=443–490 |year=1992 |issue=3 |doi=10.1007/BF02099178 |bibcode=1992CMaPh.144..443F }}</ref> Klümper, Schadschneider and Zittartz used those ideas to construct exactly solvable spin chains and coined the term ''matrix product ground states''.<ref name="kluemper">{{cite journal |last1=Klümper |first1=A. |last2=Schadschneider |first2=A. |last3=Zittartz |first3=J. |title=Matrix product ground states for one-dimensional spin-1 quantum antiferromagnets |journal=Europhysics Letters |volume=24 |pages=293–297 |year=1993 |issue=4 |doi=10.1209/0295-5075/24/4/010 |arxiv=cond-mat/9307028 |bibcode=1993EL.....24..293K }}</ref>

=== Matrix product states in nonequilibrium statistical mechanics ===
Matrix product states were also discovered independently in classical nonequilibrium statistical mechanics. In 1993 Derrida, Evans, Hakim and Pasquier solved the open [[asymmetric simple exclusion process]] (ASEP) exactly by writing its nonequilibrium steady state as a matrix product, with boundary vectors encoding the injection and extraction rates.<ref name="derrida">{{cite journal |last1=Derrida |first1=B. |last2=Evans |first2=M. R. |last3=Hakim |first3=V. |last4=Pasquier |first4=V. |title=Exact solution of a 1D asymmetric exclusion model using a matrix formulation |journal=Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and General |volume=26 |pages=1493–1517 |year=1993 |issue=7 |doi=10.1088/0305-4470/26/7/011 |bibcode=1993JPhA...26.1493D |url=https://hal.science/hal-03282962 }}</ref> This ''matrix product ansatz'' became a cornerstone of exactly solvable nonequilibrium physics: steady states of a wide range of driven diffusive systems and reaction–diffusion models admit such representations, in which infinite-dimensional matrices satisfying quadratic algebras encode long-range correlations, boundary-induced phase transitions and shock profiles.<ref name="blythe-evans">{{cite journal |last1=Blythe |first1=R. A. |last2=Evans |first2=M. R. |title=Nonequilibrium steady states of matrix-product form: a solver's guide |journal=Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and Theoretical |volume=40 |pages=R333–R441 |year=2007 |issue=46 |doi=10.1088/1751-8113/40/46/R01 |arxiv=0706.1678}}</ref> A classical stochastic generator is a special (stochastic) matrix product operator, and the ASEP algebra is a representation of the same kind of quadratic algebra that appears in the quantum transfer matrices of integrable systems. This line of work anticipated, in an exact setting, the later use of variational MPS and DMRG methods for classical stochastic dynamics and driven quantum systems.

=== DMRG and its reinterpretation ===
In 1992 — the same year as the finitely correlated states paper of Fannes, Nachtergaele and Werner — [[Steven R. White|White]] introduced the [[density matrix renormalization group]], designed to cure the failures of Wilson-style real-space RG for lattice Hamiltonians, and it rapidly became the most accurate method available for one-dimensional quantum systems. DMRG had a major impact, effectively reducing the computational complexity of many quantum-spin-chain calculations from exponential to polynomial in the system size,<ref name="dmrg30" /> and the landmark problems it solved are discussed in a separate section below.<ref name="white1992">{{cite journal |last1=White |first1=S. R. |title=Density matrix formulation for quantum renormalization groups |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=69 |pages=2863–2866 |year=1992 |issue=19 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.69.2863 |pmid=10046608 |bibcode=1992PhRvL..69.2863W }}</ref><ref name="white1993">{{cite journal |last1=White |first1=S. R. |title=Density-matrix algorithms for quantum renormalization groups |journal=Physical Review B |volume=48 |pages=10345–10356 |year=1993 |issue=14 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.48.10345 |pmid=10007313 |bibcode=1993PhRvB..4810345W }}</ref> Nishino and Okunishi connected DMRG to Baxter's corner transfer matrices, obtaining the corner transfer matrix renormalization group (CTMRG) for two-dimensional classical systems.<ref name="ctmrg">{{cite journal |last1=Nishino |first1=T. |last2=Okunishi |first2=K. |title=Corner transfer matrix renormalization group method |journal=Journal of the Physical Society of Japan |volume=65 |pages=891–894 |year=1996 |issue=4 |doi=10.1143/JPSJ.65.891 |arxiv=cond-mat/9507087 |bibcode=1996JPSJ...65..891N }}</ref> Östlund and Rommer recognized that the states produced by DMRG are matrix product states,<ref name="ostlund-rommer">{{cite journal |last1=Östlund |first1=S. |last2=Rommer |first2=S. |title=Thermodynamic limit of density matrix renormalization |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=75 |pages=3537–3540 |year=1995 |issue=19 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.75.3537 |pmid=10059611 |arxiv=cond-mat/9503107 |bibcode=1995PhRvL..75.3537O }}</ref><ref name="rommer-ostlund">{{cite journal |last1=Rommer |first1=S. |last2=Östlund |first2=S. |title=Class of ansatz wave functions for one-dimensional spin systems and their relation to the density matrix renormalization group |journal=Physical Review B |volume=55 |pages=2164–2181 |year=1997 |issue=4 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.55.2164 |arxiv=cond-mat/9606213 |bibcode=1997PhRvB..55.2164R }}</ref> and Dukelsky, Martín-Delgado, Nishino and Sierra established the equivalence of the variational matrix product method and DMRG.<ref name="dukelsky">{{cite journal |last1=Dukelsky |first1=J. |last2=Martín-Delgado |first2=M. A. |last3=Nishino |first3=T. |last4=Sierra |first4=G. |title=Equivalence of the variational matrix product method and the density matrix renormalization group applied to spin chains |journal=Europhysics Letters |volume=43 |pages=457–462 |year=1998 |issue=4 |doi=10.1209/epl/i1998-00381-x |arxiv=cond-mat/9710310 |bibcode=1998EL.....43..457D }}</ref>

=== The quantum information revolution ===
Around 2003 the field was transformed by an influx of ideas from [[quantum information theory]], which supplied both the conceptual language (entanglement, area laws, fidelity) and a toolbox of new algorithms. Vidal devised an efficient scheme for classically simulating quantum computations that generate limited entanglement, which — reinterpreted for spin chains — became the [[time-evolving block decimation]] (TEBD) algorithm and equipped DMRG with real-time dynamics.<ref name="vidal2003">{{cite journal |last1=Vidal |first1=G. |title=Efficient classical simulation of slightly entangled quantum computations |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=91 |article-number=147902 |year=2003 |issue=14 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.91.147902 |pmid=14611555 |arxiv=quant-ph/0301063 |bibcode=2003PhRvL..91n7902V }}</ref><ref name="tebd">{{cite journal |last1=Vidal |first1=G. |title=Efficient simulation of one-dimensional quantum many-body systems |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=93 |article-number=040502 |year=2004 |issue=4 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.93.040502 |pmid=15323740 |arxiv=quant-ph/0310089 |bibcode=2004PhRvL..93d0502V }}</ref><ref name="daley">{{cite journal |last1=Daley |first1=A. J. |last2=Kollath |first2=C. |last3=Schollwöck |first3=U. |last4=Vidal |first4=G. |title=Time-dependent density-matrix renormalization-group using adaptive effective Hilbert spaces |journal=Journal of Statistical Mechanics: Theory and Experiment |volume=2004 |pages=04005 |year=2004 |issue=4 |doi=10.1088/1742-5468/2004/04/P04005 |arxiv=cond-mat/0403313 |bibcode=2004JSMTE..04..005D }}</ref><ref name="white-feiguin">{{cite journal |last1=White |first1=S. R. |last2=Feiguin |first2=A. E. |title=Real-time evolution using the density matrix renormalization group |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=93 |article-number=076401 |year=2004 |issue=7 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.93.076401 |pmid=15324254 |arxiv=cond-mat/0403310 |bibcode=2004PhRvL..93g6401W }}</ref> Concurrently, work in 2004 took DMRG out of the realm of the renormalization group by recasting it as a variational optimization over the class of MPS, an interpretation that enabled many subsequent generalizations.<ref name="vpc2004">{{cite journal |last1=Verstraete |first1=F. |last2=Porras |first2=D. |last3=Cirac |first3=J. I. |title=Density matrix renormalization group and periodic boundary conditions: A quantum information perspective |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=93 |article-number=227205 |year=2004 |issue=22 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.93.227205 |pmid=15601115 |arxiv=cond-mat/0404706 |bibcode=2004PhRvL..93v7205V }}</ref> In the same year, matrix product operators (MPO) and matrix product density operators were introduced, extending the formalism to finite-temperature and dissipative dynamics,<ref name="mpdo">{{cite journal |last1=Verstraete |first1=F. |last2=García-Ripoll |first2=J. J. |last3=Cirac |first3=J. I. |title=Matrix product density operators: Simulation of finite-temperature and dissipative systems |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=93 |article-number=207204 |year=2004 |issue=20 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.93.207204 |pmid=15600964 |arxiv=cond-mat/0406426 |bibcode=2004PhRvL..93t7204V }}</ref><ref name="zwolak">{{cite journal |last1=Zwolak |first1=M. |last2=Vidal |first2=G. |title=Mixed-state dynamics in one-dimensional quantum lattice systems: A time-dependent superoperator renormalization algorithm |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=93 |article-number=207205 |year=2004 |issue=20 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.93.207205 |pmid=15600965 |arxiv=cond-mat/0406440 |bibcode=2004PhRvL..93t7205Z }}</ref> and the two-dimensional generalization of MPS was constructed. PEPS were introduced in the context of [[measurement-based quantum computation]], showing that the [[cluster state]] and related resource states are tensor networks and that measurement-based computation proceeds by steering a quantum circuit acting on the ''virtual'' entanglement degrees of freedom — an early demonstration that the virtual indices of a tensor network carry genuine computational and physical meaning.<ref name="vbs-qc">{{cite journal |last1=Verstraete |first1=F. |last2=Cirac |first2=J. I. |title=Valence-bond states for quantum computation |journal=Physical Review A |volume=70 |pages=060302(R) |year=2004 |issue=6 |article-number=060302 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.70.060302 |arxiv=quant-ph/0311130 |bibcode=2004PhRvA..70f0302V }}</ref> The companion paper formulated PEPS as a general variational family for two- and higher-dimensional quantum systems and provided the algorithms for optimizing them in the form of boundary-MPS methods.<ref name="peps" />

=== Hierarchical tensor networks ===
[[File:TTN diagram.svg|thumb|upright=1.6|A tree tensor network on sixteen sites: the physical indices sit at the leaves of the tree, and the successive layers implement a real-space coarse-graining terminating in a top tensor.]]
[[File:MERA diagram.svg|thumb|upright=1.6|The multiscale entanglement renormalization ansatz (MERA): layers of disentanglers (squares) and isometries (triangles) implement a real-space renormalization group flow. Unlike a tree tensor network, the disentanglers remove short-range entanglement between neighbouring blocks before each coarse-graining step.]]
Vidal subsequently introduced the [[multiscale entanglement renormalization ansatz]] (MERA), a hierarchical tensor network incorporating disentanglers, designed to capture the scale invariance of critical systems and to realize a genuine real-space renormalization group flow on quantum states;<ref name="mera1">{{cite journal |last1=Vidal |first1=G. |title=Entanglement renormalization |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=99 |article-number=220405 |year=2007 |issue=22 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.99.220405 |pmid=18233268 |arxiv=cond-mat/0512165 |bibcode=2007PhRvL..99v0405V }}</ref><ref name="mera2">{{cite journal |last1=Vidal |first1=G. |title=Class of quantum many-body states that can be efficiently simulated |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=101 |article-number=110501 |year=2008 |issue=11 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.101.110501 |pmid=18851269 |arxiv=quant-ph/0610099 |bibcode=2008PhRvL.101k0501V }}</ref> practical algorithms were developed with Evenbly.<ref name="evenbly-vidal">{{cite journal |last1=Evenbly |first1=G. |last2=Vidal |first2=G. |title=Algorithms for entanglement renormalization |journal=Physical Review B |volume=79 |article-number=144108 |year=2009 |issue=14 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.79.144108 |arxiv=0707.1454 |bibcode=2009PhRvB..79n4108E }}</ref> Precursors of the underlying coarse-graining structure can be found in the strong-disorder renormalization group of Dasgupta and Ma.<ref name="dasgupta-ma">{{cite journal |last1=Dasgupta |first1=C. |last2=Ma |first2=S.-k. |title=Low-temperature properties of the random Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chain |journal=Physical Review B |volume=22 |pages=1305–1319 |year=1980 |issue=3 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.22.1305 |bibcode=1980PhRvB..22.1305D }}</ref> Tree tensor networks, hierarchical networks without disentanglers, were developed in parallel by several groups.<ref name="ttn-shi">{{cite journal |last1=Shi |first1=Y.-Y. |last2=Duan |first2=L.-M. |last3=Vidal |first3=G. |title=Classical simulation of quantum many-body systems with a tree tensor network |journal=Physical Review A |volume=74 |article-number=022320 |year=2006 |issue=2 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.74.022320 |arxiv=quant-ph/0511070 |bibcode=2006PhRvA..74b2320S }}</ref><ref name="ttn-silvi">{{cite journal |last1=Silvi |first1=P. |last2=Giovannetti |first2=V. |last3=Montangero |first3=S. |last4=Rizzi |first4=M. |last5=Cirac |first5=J. I. |last6=Fazio |first6=R. |title=Homogeneous binary trees as ground states of quantum critical Hamiltonians |journal=Physical Review A |volume=81 |article-number=062335 |year=2010 |issue=6 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.81.062335 |arxiv=0912.0466 |bibcode=2010PhRvA..81f2335S }}</ref>

Essentially the same low-rank decompositions were later discovered in numerical mathematics: the tensor train decomposition of Oseledets is an MPS, and the hierarchical Tucker format of Hackbusch and Kühn is a tree tensor network.<ref name="oseledets">{{cite journal |last1=Oseledets |first1=I. V. |title=Tensor-train decomposition |journal=SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing |volume=33 |pages=2295–2317 |year=2011 |issue=5 |doi=10.1137/090752286 |bibcode=2011SJSC...33.2295O }}</ref><ref name="hackbusch">{{cite journal |last1=Hackbusch |first1=W. |last2=Kühn |first2=S. |title=A new scheme for the tensor representation |journal=Journal of Fourier Analysis and Applications |volume=15 |pages=706–722 |year=2009 |issue=5 |doi=10.1007/s00041-009-9094-9 |bibcode=2009JFAA...15..706H |doi-access=free }}</ref> This has led to a large parallel literature on tensor decompositions and networks for high-dimensional problems in applied mathematics, signal processing and scientific computing.<ref name="kolda-bader">{{cite journal |last1=Kolda |first1=T. G. |last2=Bader |first2=B. W. |title=Tensor decompositions and applications |journal=SIAM Review |volume=51 |issue=3 |pages=455–500 |year=2009 |doi=10.1137/07070111X |bibcode=2009SIAMR..51..455K }}</ref><ref name="cichocki" />
=== Landmark results ===
The immediate impact of DMRG came from the problems it solved. Shortly after introducing the method, White and Huse computed the [[Haldane gap]] of the spin-1 Heisenberg chain to five-digit accuracy — and its ground-state energy per site to essentially machine precision — providing a high-precision numerical confirmation of the Haldane conjecture and setting a new standard of numerical accuracy for correlated lattice models.<ref name="white-huse">{{cite journal |last1=White |first1=S. R. |last2=Huse |first2=D. A. |title=Numerical renormalization-group study of low-lying eigenstates of the antiferromagnetic S=1 Heisenberg chain |journal=Physical Review B |volume=48 |pages=3844–3852 |year=1993 |issue=6 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.48.3844 |pmid=10008834 |bibcode=1993PhRvB..48.3844W }}</ref>

The method was soon extended from static to dynamical properties, giving access to the spectral functions measured in neutron scattering and photoemission experiments: Hallberg introduced continued-fraction (Lanczos) techniques,<ref name="hallberg">{{cite journal |last1=Hallberg |first1=K. A. |title=Density-matrix algorithm for the calculation of dynamical properties of low-dimensional systems |journal=Physical Review B |volume=52 |pages=R9827–R9830 |year=1995 |issue=14 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.52.R9827 |pmid=9980124 |arxiv=cond-mat/9503094 |bibcode=1995PhRvB..52.9827H }}</ref> Kühner and White developed the correction-vector method,<ref name="kuehner-white">{{cite journal |last1=Kühner |first1=T. D. |last2=White |first2=S. R. |title=Dynamical correlation functions using the density matrix renormalization group |journal=Physical Review B |volume=60 |pages=335–343 |year=1999 |issue=1 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.60.335 |arxiv=cond-mat/9812372 |bibcode=1999PhRvB..60..335K }}</ref> and Jeckelmann reformulated the computation of spectral functions as a variational minimization — the dynamical DMRG — enabling momentum- and frequency-resolved spectra of strongly correlated chains with an accuracy rivalling experiment.<ref name="jeckelmann">{{cite journal |last1=Jeckelmann |first1=E. |title=Dynamical density-matrix renormalization-group method |journal=Physical Review B |volume=66 |article-number=045114 |year=2002 |issue=4 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.66.045114 |arxiv=cond-mat/0203500 |bibcode=2002PhRvB..66d5114J }}</ref> The introduction of real-time evolution<ref name="tebd" /><ref name="daley" /><ref name="white-feiguin" /> and of minimally entangled typical thermal states (METTS) for finite temperature<ref name="metts">{{cite journal |last1=White |first1=S. R. |title=Minimally entangled typical quantum states at finite temperature |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=102 |article-number=190601 |year=2009 |issue=19 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.102.190601 |pmid=19518934 |arxiv=0902.4475 |bibcode=2009PhRvL.102s0601W }}</ref><ref name="feiguin-white" /> extended the numerical toolbox.

DMRG on ladders and cylinders subsequently settled major open problems in two-dimensional physics. White and Scalapino discovered stripe order in the two-dimensional t–J model,<ref name="white-scalapino">{{cite journal |last1=White |first1=S. R. |last2=Scalapino |first2=D. J. |title=Density matrix renormalization group study of the striped phase in the 2D t-J model |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=80 |pages=1272–1275 |year=1998 |issue=6 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.80.1272 |arxiv=cond-mat/9705128 |bibcode=1998PhRvL..80.1272W }}</ref> a result central to the physics of the cuprate superconductors and later confirmed for the Hubbard model in a landmark multi-method benchmark.<ref name="zheng" /> Yan, Huse and White produced the first strong numerical evidence for a spin-liquid ground state of the spin-1/2 kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet,<ref name="yan-huse-white">{{cite journal |last1=Yan |first1=S. |last2=Huse |first2=D. A. |last3=White |first3=S. R. |title=Spin-liquid ground state of the S=1/2 kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet |journal=Science |volume=332 |pages=1173–1176 |year=2011 |issue=6034 |doi=10.1126/science.1201080 |pmid=21527676 |arxiv=1011.6114 |bibcode=2011Sci...332.1173Y }}</ref> a milestone in the study of frustrated magnetism.

White also carried the method far beyond spin chains: with Martin he generalized DMRG to ''ab initio'' quantum chemistry by treating molecular orbitals as the sites of a fictitious lattice,<ref name="white-martin" /> a development pushed further by Legeza, by Chan and by Yanai and collaborators — the DMRG study of the notoriously multireference chromium dimer being an emblematic success<ref name="legeza" /><ref name="chan" /><ref name="kurashige">{{cite journal |last1=Kurashige |first1=Y. |last2=Yanai |first2=T. |title=Second-order perturbation theory with a density matrix renormalization group self-consistent field reference function: Theory and application to the study of chromium dimer |journal=Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=135 |article-number=094104 |year=2011 |issue=9 |doi=10.1063/1.3629454 |pmid=21913750 |bibcode=2011JChPh.135i4104K }}</ref> — so that DMRG is now a standard tool for strongly correlated molecules and active spaces. Through the variational MPS reformulation of the numerical renormalization group, the same technology also subsumed and improved Wilson's treatment of quantum impurity problems.<ref name="weichselbaum" />

== Algorithms ==

=== Matrix product state methods ===
DMRG remains the workhorse algorithm of the field. Although originally formulated in renormalization group language inspired by the numerical renormalization group,<ref name="white1992" /> the modern view — expounded in the review "The density-matrix renormalization group in the age of matrix product states" — is that DMRG is an alternating least squares variational optimization over the MPS manifold, with only a loose connection to renormalization ideas.<ref name="vpc2004" /><ref name="schollwoeck2011">{{cite journal |last1=Schollwöck |first1=U. |title=The density-matrix renormalization group in the age of matrix product states |journal=Annals of Physics |volume=326 |pages=96–192 |year=2011 |issue=1 |doi=10.1016/j.aop.2010.09.012 |arxiv=1008.3477 |bibcode=2011AnPhy.326...96S }}</ref> The corner transfer matrix renormalization group, rooted in Baxter's corner transfer matrices, plays the analogous role for two-dimensional tensor contractions and was later adapted to the contraction of infinite PEPS.<ref name="ctmrg" /><ref name="orus-vidal-ctmrg">{{cite journal |last1=Orús |first1=R. |last2=Vidal |first2=G. |title=Simulation of two-dimensional quantum systems on an infinite lattice revisited: Corner transfer matrix for tensor contraction |journal=Physical Review B |volume=80 |article-number=094403 |year=2009 |issue=9 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.80.094403 |arxiv=0905.3225 |bibcode=2009PhRvB..80i4403O }}</ref>

Real-time evolution can be performed with TEBD<ref name="tebd" /> and its variants,<ref name="daley" /><ref name="white-feiguin" /> while finite-temperature and dissipative dynamics use matrix product operators.<ref name="mpdo" /><ref name="zwolak" /><ref name="feiguin-white">{{cite journal |last1=Feiguin |first1=A. E. |last2=White |first2=S. R. |title=Finite-temperature density matrix renormalization using an enlarged Hilbert space |journal=Physical Review B |volume=72 |pages=220401(R) |year=2005 |issue=22 |article-number=220401 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.72.220401 |arxiv=cond-mat/0510124 |bibcode=2005PhRvB..72v0401F }}</ref> Matrix product operators also give exact compact representations of local Hamiltonians themselves, including those with long-range interactions, a structure that can be understood in terms of finite-state automata.<ref name="pirvu-mpo">{{cite journal |last1=Pirvu |first1=B. |last2=Murg |first2=V. |last3=Cirac |first3=J. I. |last4=Verstraete |first4=F. |title=Matrix product operator representations |journal=New Journal of Physics |volume=12 |article-number=025012 |year=2010 |issue=2 |doi=10.1088/1367-2630/12/2/025012 |arxiv=0804.3976 |bibcode=2010NJPh...12b5012P }}</ref><ref name="crosswhite">{{cite journal |last1=Crosswhite |first1=G. M. |last2=Bacon |first2=D. |title=Finite automata for caching in matrix product algorithms |journal=Physical Review A |volume=78 |article-number=012356 |year=2008 |issue=1 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.78.012356 |arxiv=0708.1221 |bibcode=2008PhRvA..78a2356C }}</ref><ref name="mcculloch">{{cite journal |last1=McCulloch |first1=I. P. |title=From density-matrix renormalization group to matrix product states |journal=Journal of Statistical Mechanics: Theory and Experiment |volume=2007 |article-number=10014 |year=2007 |issue=10 |doi=10.1088/1742-5468/2007/10/P10014 |arxiv=cond-mat/0701428 |bibcode=2007JSMTE..10...14M }}</ref> Several of these ingredients — MPS bond-dimension reduction, time evolution implemented by MPOs, and alternating least-squares sweeps — also appear in the original PEPS paper.<ref name="peps" />

Continuous matrix product states (cMPS) extend the variational class to quantum fields in the continuum.<ref name="cmps">{{cite journal |last1=Verstraete |first1=F. |last2=Cirac |first2=J. I. |title=Continuous matrix product states for quantum fields |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=104 |article-number=190405 |year=2010 |issue=19 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.104.190405 |pmid=20866951 |arxiv=1002.1824 |bibcode=2010PhRvL.104s0405V }}</ref> Because Trotter-based methods such as TEBD rely on truncations that are ill-defined in the continuum limit and can break the symmetries of the ansatz, a [[time-dependent variational principle]] (TDVP) for cMPS was developed and later adapted to the usual MPS setting: time evolution is projected onto the tangent space of the variational manifold, yielding a symplectic flow on the (Kähler) manifold of MPS that exactly conserves energy and preserves symmetries.<ref name="tdvp2011">{{cite journal |last1=Haegeman |first1=J. |last2=Cirac |first2=J. I. |last3=Osborne |first3=T. J. |last4=Pižorn |first4=I. |last5=Verschelde |first5=H. |last6=Verstraete |first6=F. |title=Time-dependent variational principle for quantum lattices |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=107 |article-number=070601 |year=2011 |issue=7 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.107.070601 |pmid=21902379 |arxiv=1103.0936 |bibcode=2011PhRvL.107g0601H }}</ref> Combined with projector-splitting integrators developed in the numerical analysis community — where gauge choices are exploited to make the metric on the manifold effectively flat — this has become a widely used approach to MPS time evolution.<ref name="lubich">{{cite journal |last1=Lubich |first1=C. |last2=Oseledets |first2=I. V. |last3=Vandereycken |first3=B. |title=Time integration of tensor trains |journal=SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis |volume=53 |pages=917–941 |year=2015 |issue=2 |doi=10.1137/140976546 |arxiv=1407.2042}}</ref><ref name="tdvp-unifying">{{cite journal |last1=Haegeman |first1=J. |last2=Lubich |first2=C. |last3=Oseledets |first3=I. |last4=Vandereycken |first4=B. |last5=Verstraete |first5=F. |title=Unifying time evolution and optimization with matrix product states |journal=Physical Review B |volume=94 |article-number=165116 |year=2016 |issue=16 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.94.165116 |arxiv=1408.5056 |bibcode=2016PhRvB..94p5116H }}</ref> For translation-invariant systems the VUMPS ("variational uniform matrix product states") algorithm optimizes uniform MPS directly in the thermodynamic limit.<ref name="vumps">{{cite journal |last1=Zauner-Stauber |first1=V. |last2=Vanderstraeten |first2=L. |last3=Fishman |first3=M. T. |last4=Verstraete |first4=F. |last5=Haegeman |first5=J. |title=Variational optimization algorithms for uniform matrix product states |journal=Physical Review B |volume=97 |article-number=045145 |year=2018 |issue=4 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.97.045145 |arxiv=1701.07035 |bibcode=2018PhRvB..97d5145Z }}</ref>

These developments are unified by ''tangent-space methods'', which treat the set of uniform MPS as a differentiable manifold embedded in Hilbert space.<ref name="tangent-review">{{cite journal |last1=Vanderstraeten |first1=L. |last2=Haegeman |first2=J. |last3=Verstraete |first3=F. |title=Tangent-space methods for uniform matrix product states |journal=SciPost Physics Lecture Notes |volume=7 |year=2019 |article-number=7 |doi=10.21468/SciPostPhysLectNotes.7 |doi-access=free |arxiv=1810.07006}}</ref> Elementary excitations are captured by the excitation ansatz — plane-wave superpositions of local perturbations of the ground state MPS — an idea whose roots go back to the earliest variational formulations of DMRG<ref name="rommer-ostlund" /> and which was made into a practical, quantitatively accurate method by tangent-space techniques,<ref name="excitation">{{cite journal |last1=Haegeman |first1=J. |last2=Pirvu |first2=B. |last3=Weir |first3=D. J. |last4=Cirac |first4=J. I. |last5=Osborne |first5=T. J. |last6=Verschelde |first6=H. |last7=Verstraete |first7=F. |title=Variational matrix product ansatz for dispersion relations |journal=Physical Review B |volume=85 |pages=100408(R) |year=2012 |issue=10 |article-number=100408 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.85.100408 |arxiv=1103.2286 |bibcode=2012PhRvB..85j0408H }}</ref> which have been extended to the computation of scattering matrices of these excitations.<ref name="smatrix">{{cite journal |last1=Vanderstraeten |first1=L. |last2=Haegeman |first2=J. |last3=Osborne |first3=T. J. |last4=Verstraete |first4=F. |title=S matrix from matrix product states |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=112 |article-number=257202 |year=2014 |issue=25 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.112.257202 |pmid=25014826 |arxiv=1312.6793 |bibcode=2014PhRvL.112y7202V }}</ref>

The formalism extends beyond spin systems. Fermionic and graded tensor networks incorporate fermionic statistics directly at the level of the tensors.<ref name="fermionic-mps">{{cite journal |last1=Bultinck |first1=N. |last2=Williamson |first2=D. J. |last3=Haegeman |first3=J. |last4=Verstraete |first4=F. |title=Fermionic matrix product states and one-dimensional topological phases |journal=Physical Review B |volume=95 |article-number=075108 |year=2017 |issue=7 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.95.075108 |arxiv=1610.07849 |bibcode=2017PhRvB..95g5108B }}</ref> Matrix product states have been applied extensively to lattice gauge theories, beginning with precision studies of the Schwinger model and the explicit construction of gauge-invariant MPS.<ref name="banuls-schwinger">{{cite journal |last1=Bañuls |first1=M. C. |last2=Cichy |first2=K. |last3=Cirac |first3=J. I. |last4=Jansen |first4=K. |title=The mass spectrum of the Schwinger model with matrix product states |journal=Journal of High Energy Physics |volume=2013 |issue=11 |pages=158 |year=2013 |doi=10.1007/JHEP11(2013)158 |arxiv=1305.3765 |bibcode=2013JHEP...11..158B }}</ref><ref name="buyens">{{cite journal |last1=Buyens |first1=B. |last2=Haegeman |first2=J. |last3=Van Acoleyen |first3=K. |last4=Verschelde |first4=H. |last5=Verstraete |first5=F. |title=Matrix product states for gauge field theories |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=113 |article-number=091601 |year=2014 |issue=9 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.113.091601 |pmid=25215973 |arxiv=1312.6654 |bibcode=2014PhRvL.113i1601B }}</ref><ref name="banuls-lgt">{{cite journal |last1=Bañuls |first1=M. C. |display-authors=etal |title=Simulating lattice gauge theories within quantum technologies |journal=European Physical Journal D |volume=74 |article-number=165 |year=2020 |issue=8 |doi=10.1140/epjd/e2020-100571-8 |arxiv=1911.00003 |bibcode=2020EPJD...74..165B }}</ref> In quantum chemistry, DMRG applied to the orbital chain has become a standard tool for strongly correlated molecules (see the dedicated section below), and DMRG on cylinders is a leading method for two-dimensional lattice models.<ref name="stoudenmire-white">{{cite journal |last1=Stoudenmire |first1=E. M. |last2=White |first2=S. R. |title=Studying two-dimensional systems with the density matrix renormalization group |journal=Annual Review of Condensed Matter Physics |volume=3 |pages=111–128 |year=2012 |doi=10.1146/annurev-conmatphys-020911-125018 |arxiv=1105.1374}}</ref>

=== DMRG for quantum chemistry ===
The generalization of DMRG to ''ab initio'' quantum chemistry treats the molecular orbitals of the full quantum chemical Hamiltonian as the sites of a one-dimensional lattice.<ref name="white-martin">{{cite journal |last1=White |first1=S. R. |last2=Martin |first2=R. L. |title=Ab initio quantum chemistry using the density matrix renormalization group |journal=Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=110 |pages=4127–4130 |year=1999 |issue=9 |doi=10.1063/1.478295 |arxiv=cond-mat/9808118 |bibcode=1999JChPh.110.4127W }}</ref> Early independent implementations followed,<ref name="mitrushenkov">{{cite journal |last1=Mitrushenkov |first1=A. O. |last2=Fano |first2=G. |last3=Ortolani |first3=F. |last4=Linguerri |first4=R. |last5=Palmieri |first5=P. |title=Quantum chemistry using the density matrix renormalization group |journal=Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=115 |pages=6815–6821 |year=2001 |issue=15 |doi=10.1063/1.1389475 |bibcode=2001JChPh.115.6815M }}</ref> and highly efficient polynomial-cost implementations soon delivered essentially exact (full configuration interaction quality) energies for small molecules.<ref name="chan-headgordon">{{cite journal |last1=Chan |first1=G. K.-L. |last2=Head-Gordon |first2=M. |title=Highly correlated calculations with a polynomial cost algorithm: A study of the density matrix renormalization group |journal=Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=116 |pages=4462–4476 |year=2002 |issue=11 |doi=10.1063/1.1449459 |bibcode=2002JChPh.116.4462C }}</ref> The dynamical block state selection protocol was introduced to control the truncation error<ref name="legeza">{{cite journal |last1=Legeza |first1=Ö. |last2=Röder |first2=J. |last3=Hess |first3=B. A. |title=Controlling the accuracy of the density-matrix renormalization-group method: The dynamical block state selection approach |journal=Physical Review B |volume=67 |article-number=125114 |year=2003 |issue=12 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.67.125114 |arxiv=cond-mat/0204602 |bibcode=2003PhRvB..67l5114L }}</ref> and the use of quantum information measures — orbital entropies and mutual information — to order and select the orbitals has become standard practice.<ref name="legeza-solyom">{{cite journal |last1=Legeza |first1=Ö. |last2=Sólyom |first2=J. |title=Optimizing the density-matrix renormalization group method using quantum information entropy |journal=Physical Review B |volume=68 |article-number=195116 |year=2003 |issue=19 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.68.195116 |arxiv=cond-mat/0305336 |bibcode=2003PhRvB..68s5116L }}</ref> Further methodological milestones include spin-adapted formulations,<ref name="sharma-chan-spin">{{cite journal |last1=Sharma |first1=S. |last2=Chan |first2=G. K.-L. |title=Spin-adapted density matrix renormalization group algorithms for quantum chemistry |journal=Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=136 |article-number=124121 |year=2012 |issue=12 |doi=10.1063/1.3695642 |pmid=22462849 |arxiv=1408.5039 |bibcode=2012JChPh.136l4121S }}</ref> efficient matrix product operator representations of the quantum chemical Hamiltonian,<ref name="qcmaquis-mpo">{{cite journal |last1=Keller |first1=S. |last2=Dolfi |first2=M. |last3=Troyer |first3=M. |last4=Reiher |first4=M. |title=An efficient matrix product operator representation of the quantum chemical Hamiltonian |journal=Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=143 |article-number=244118 |year=2015 |issue=24 |doi=10.1063/1.4939000 |pmid=26723662 |arxiv=1510.02026 |bibcode=2015JChPh.143x4118K }}</ref> and hybrid schemes such as coupled cluster theory tailored by matrix product states.<ref name="veis-tcc">{{cite journal |last1=Veis |first1=L. |last2=Antalík |first2=A. |last3=Brabec |first3=J. |last4=Neese |first4=F. |last5=Legeza |first5=Ö. |last6=Pittner |first6=J. |title=Coupled cluster method with single and double excitations tailored by matrix product state wave functions |journal=Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters |volume=7 |pages=4072–4078 |year=2016 |issue=20 |doi=10.1021/acs.jpclett.6b01908 |pmid=27682626 |arxiv=1606.06002 |bibcode=2016JPCL....7.4072V }}</ref>

Because its cost is insensitive to the multireference character of the wavefunction, DMRG opened active spaces of 50–100 orbitals — far beyond the reach of conventional complete active space methods — and thereby gave access to the electronic structure of polynuclear transition-metal complexes. Pioneering applications addressed the relative energies of transition-metal complexes and clusters,<ref name="marti-reiher">{{cite journal |last1=Marti |first1=K. H. |last2=Malkin Ondík |first2=I. |last3=Moritz |first3=G. |last4=Reiher |first4=M. |title=Density matrix renormalization group calculations on relative energies of transition metal complexes and clusters |journal=Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=128 |article-number=014104 |year=2008 |issue=1 |doi=10.1063/1.2805383 |pmid=18190182 |bibcode=2008JChPh.128a4104M }}</ref> later work resolved the entangled electronic structure of the Mn<sub>4</sub>CaO<sub>5</sub> cluster of photosystem II,<ref name="kurashige-psii">{{cite journal |last1=Kurashige |first1=Y. |last2=Chan |first2=G. K.-L. |last3=Yanai |first3=T. |title=Entangled quantum electronic wavefunctions of the Mn4CaO5 cluster in photosystem II |journal=Nature Chemistry |volume=5 |pages=660–666 |year=2013 |issue=8 |doi=10.1038/nchem.1677 |pmid=23881496 }}</ref> and DMRG calculations on the FeMo cofactor of nitrogenase — first used to define the benchmark problem for future quantum computers,<ref name="reiher-femoco">{{cite journal |last1=Reiher |first1=M. |last2=Wiebe |first2=N. |last3=Svore |first3=K. M. |last4=Wecker |first4=D. |last5=Troyer |first5=M. |title=Elucidating reaction mechanisms on quantum computers |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=114 |pages=7555–7560 |year=2017 |issue=29 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1619152114 |doi-access=free |pmid=28674011 |pmc=5530650 |arxiv=1605.03590 |bibcode=2017PNAS..114.7555R }}</ref> then carried out in earnest for the FeMo cofactor and the P-cluster — mapped the low-energy landscape of the most demanding electronic structure problems in biochemistry.<ref name="li-chan-femoco">{{cite journal |last1=Li |first1=Z. |last2=Li |first2=J. |last3=Dattani |first3=N. S. |last4=Umrigar |first4=C. J. |last5=Chan |first5=G. K.-L. |title=The electronic complexity of the ground-state of the FeMo cofactor of nitrogenase as relevant to quantum simulations |journal=Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=150 |article-number=024302 |year=2019 |issue=2 |doi=10.1063/1.5063376 |pmid=30646701 |arxiv=1809.10307 |bibcode=2019JChPh.150b4302L }}</ref><ref name="li-chan-pcluster">{{cite journal |last1=Li |first1=Z. |last2=Guo |first2=S. |last3=Sun |first3=Q. |last4=Chan |first4=G. K.-L. |title=Electronic landscape of the P-cluster of nitrogenase as revealed through many-electron quantum wavefunction simulations |journal=Nature Chemistry |volume=11 |pages=1026–1033 |year=2019 |issue=11 |doi=10.1038/s41557-019-0337-3 |pmid=31570817 |arxiv=1810.10196 |bibcode=2019NatCh..11.1026L }}</ref> Mature open-source implementations include Block2,<ref name="block2">{{cite journal |last1=Zhai |first1=H. |last2=Larsson |first2=H. R. |last3=Lee |first3=S. |last4=Cui |first4=Z.-H. |last5=Zhu |first5=T. |last6=Sun |first6=C. |last7=Peng |first7=L. |last8=Peng |first8=R. |last9=Liao |first9=K. |last10=Tölle |first10=J. |last11=Yang |first11=J. |last12=Li |first12=S. |last13=Chan |first13=G. K.-L. |title=Block2: A comprehensive open source framework to develop and apply state-of-the-art DMRG algorithms in electronic structure and beyond |journal=Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=159 |article-number=234801 |year=2023 |issue=23 |doi=10.1063/5.0180424 |pmid=38108484 |arxiv=2310.03920 |bibcode=2023JChPh.159w4801Z }}</ref> CheMPS2,<ref name="chemps2">{{cite journal |last1=Wouters |first1=S. |last2=Poelmans |first2=W. |last3=Ayers |first3=P. W. |last4=Van Neck |first4=D. |title=CheMPS2: A free open-source spin-adapted implementation of the density matrix renormalization group for ab initio quantum chemistry |journal=Computer Physics Communications |volume=185 |pages=1501–1514 |year=2014 |issue=6 |doi=10.1016/j.cpc.2014.01.019 |arxiv=1312.2415 |bibcode=2014CoPhC.185.1501W }}</ref> and QCMaquis; the state of the field is surveyed in dedicated reviews.<ref name="chan">{{cite journal |last1=Chan |first1=G. K.-L. |last2=Sharma |first2=S. |title=The density matrix renormalization group in quantum chemistry |journal=Annual Review of Physical Chemistry |volume=62 |pages=465–481 |year=2011 |doi=10.1146/annurev-physchem-032210-103338 |pmid=21219144 |bibcode=2011ARPC...62..465C }}</ref><ref name="baiardi-reiher">{{cite journal |last1=Baiardi |first1=A. |last2=Reiher |first2=M. |title=The density matrix renormalization group in chemistry and molecular physics: Recent developments and new challenges |journal=Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=152 |article-number=040903 |year=2020 |issue=4 |doi=10.1063/1.5129672 |pmid=32007028 |arxiv=1910.00137 |bibcode=2020JChPh.152d0903B }}</ref>

=== PEPS methods ===
[[File:PEPS diagram.svg|thumb|upright=1.4|A projected entangled pair state (PEPS) on a 6×6 square lattice: each tensor carries one physical index (diagonal leg) and up to four virtual indices connecting it to its nearest neighbours, so that the entanglement entropy of any region automatically satisfies an area law.]]
The essential algorithmic toolbox for two-dimensional tensor networks involves the contraction of the network by boundary MPS, imaginary-time evolution implemented through MPOs acting on the PEPS (the "full update"), and variational sweeping by alternating least squares.<ref name="peps" /> Exact contraction of a generic PEPS is a computationally hard ([[Sharp-P|#P-complete]]) problem,<ref name="peps-complexity">{{cite journal |last1=Schuch |first1=N. |last2=Wolf |first2=M. M. |last3=Verstraete |first3=F. |last4=Cirac |first4=J. I. |title=Computational complexity of projected entangled pair states |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=98 |article-number=140506 |year=2007 |issue=14 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.98.140506 |pmid=17501258 |arxiv=quant-ph/0611050 |bibcode=2007PhRvL..98n0506S }}</ref> so all practical PEPS algorithms rest on approximate contraction; rigorous global error bounds are generally not available, and in practice the accuracy of an environment approximation is assessed by increasing its dimension and monitoring convergence. Contemporaneously with the original PEPS work, closely related tensor product variational formulations had been developed for three-dimensional classical statistical mechanics.<ref name="nishino-3d">{{cite journal |last1=Nishino |first1=T. |last2=Hieida |first2=Y. |last3=Okunishi |first3=K. |last4=Maeshima |first4=N. |last5=Akutsu |first5=Y. |last6=Gendiar |first6=A. |title=Two-dimensional tensor product variational formulation |journal=Progress of Theoretical Physics |volume=105 |pages=409–417 |year=2001 |issue=3 |doi=10.1143/PTP.105.409 |arxiv=cond-mat/0011103 |bibcode=2001PThPh.105..409N }}</ref>

The extension to infinite, translation-invariant systems (iPEPS) followed soon afterwards.<ref name="ipeps">{{cite journal |last1=Jordan |first1=J. |last2=Orús |first2=R. |last3=Vidal |first3=G. |last4=Verstraete |first4=F. |last5=Cirac |first5=J. I. |title=Classical simulation of infinite-size quantum lattice systems in two spatial dimensions |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=101 |article-number=250602 |year=2008 |issue=25 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.101.250602 |pmid=19113687 |arxiv=cond-mat/0703788 |bibcode=2008PhRvL.101y0602J }}</ref> The "simple update", a cheap local truncation scheme, was introduced next,<ref name="simple-update">{{cite journal |last1=Jiang |first1=H. C. |last2=Weng |first2=Z. Y. |last3=Xiang |first3=T. |title=Accurate determination of tensor network state of quantum lattice models in two dimensions |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=101 |article-number=090603 |year=2008 |issue=9 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.101.090603 |pmid=18851596 |arxiv=0806.3719 |bibcode=2008PhRvL.101i0603J }}</ref> and CTMRG-based contraction was developed into the standard environment computation for iPEPS, including for fermionic systems.<ref name="orus-vidal-ctmrg" /><ref name="corboz-ctmrg">{{cite journal |last1=Corboz |first1=P. |last2=White |first2=S. R. |last3=Vidal |first3=G. |last4=Troyer |first4=M. |title=Stripes in the two-dimensional t-J model with infinite projected entangled-pair states |journal=Physical Review B |volume=84 |pages=041108(R) |year=2011 |issue=4 |article-number=041108 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.84.041108 |arxiv=1104.5463 |bibcode=2011PhRvB..84d1108C }}</ref> PEPS simulations of fermions encode the fermionic exchange signs algebraically in the tensors, and therefore do not encounter the statistical [[Numerical sign problem|sign problem]] that plagues quantum Monte Carlo. Fermionic tensor networks were formulated directly, first for fermionic PEPS<ref name="kraus-fpeps">{{cite journal |last1=Kraus |first1=C. V. |last2=Schuch |first2=N. |last3=Verstraete |first3=F. |last4=Cirac |first4=J. I. |title=Fermionic projected entangled pair states |journal=Physical Review A |volume=81 |article-number=052338 |year=2010 |issue=5 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.81.052338 |arxiv=0904.4667 |bibcode=2010PhRvA..81e2338K }}</ref> and fermionic entanglement renormalization,<ref name="corboz-evv">{{cite journal |last1=Corboz |first1=P. |last2=Evenbly |first2=G. |last3=Verstraete |first3=F. |last4=Vidal |first4=G. |title=Simulation of interacting fermions with entanglement renormalization |journal=Physical Review A |volume=81 |pages=010303(R) |year=2010 |issue=1 |article-number=010303 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.81.010303 |arxiv=0904.4151 |bibcode=2010PhRvA..81a0303C }}</ref> followed shortly afterwards by further formulations<ref name="pizorn-fpeps">{{cite journal |last1=Pižorn |first1=I. |last2=Verstraete |first2=F. |title=Fermionic implementation of projected entangled pair states algorithm |journal=Physical Review B |volume=81 |article-number=245110 |year=2010 |issue=24 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.81.245110 |arxiv=1003.2743 |bibcode=2010PhRvB..81x5110P }}</ref> and simulations of strongly correlated fermions.<ref name="corboz-fermions">{{cite journal |last1=Corboz |first1=P. |last2=Orús |first2=R. |last3=Bauer |first3=B. |last4=Vidal |first4=G. |title=Simulation of strongly correlated fermions in two spatial dimensions with fermionic projected entangled-pair states |journal=Physical Review B |volume=81 |article-number=165104 |year=2010 |issue=16 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.81.165104 |arxiv=0912.0646 |bibcode=2010PhRvB..81p5104C }}</ref> Modern implementations are based on Grassmann or graded (super vector space) tensor networks.<ref name="grassmann">{{cite arXiv |last1=Gu |first1=Z.-C. |last2=Verstraete |first2=F. |last3=Wen |first3=X.-G. |title=Grassmann tensor network states and its renormalization for strongly correlated fermionic and bosonic states |year=2010 |class=cond-mat.str-el |eprint=1004.2563}}</ref><ref name="mortier">{{cite journal |last1=Mortier |first1=Q. |last2=Devos |first2=L. |last3=Burgelman |first3=L. |last4=Vanhecke |first4=B. |last5=Bultinck |first5=N. |last6=Verstraete |first6=F. |last7=Haegeman |first7=J. |last8=Vanderstraeten |first8=L. |title=Fermionic tensor network methods |journal=SciPost Physics |volume=18 |article-number=012 |year=2025 |issue=1 |doi=10.21468/SciPostPhys.18.1.012 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2025ScPP...18...12M }}</ref>

Modern methods for variational iPEPS optimization include energy-gradient methods,<ref name="grad-vdstr">{{cite journal |last1=Vanderstraeten |first1=L. |last2=Haegeman |first2=J. |last3=Corboz |first3=P. |last4=Verstraete |first4=F. |title=Gradient methods for variational optimization of projected entangled-pair states |journal=Physical Review B |volume=94 |article-number=155123 |year=2016 |issue=15 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.94.155123 |arxiv=1606.09170 |bibcode=2016PhRvB..94o5123V }}</ref><ref name="grad-corboz">{{cite journal |last1=Corboz |first1=P. |title=Variational optimization with infinite projected entangled-pair states |journal=Physical Review B |volume=94 |article-number=035133 |year=2016 |issue=3 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.94.035133 |arxiv=1605.03006 |bibcode=2016PhRvB..94c5133C }}</ref> made considerably more convenient by automatic differentiation borrowed from machine learning,<ref name="autodiff">{{cite journal |last1=Liao |first1=H.-J. |last2=Liu |first2=J.-G. |last3=Wang |first3=L. |last4=Xiang |first4=T. |title=Differentiable programming tensor networks |journal=Physical Review X |volume=9 |article-number=031041 |year=2019 |issue=3 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevX.9.031041 |arxiv=1903.09650 |bibcode=2019PhRvX...9c1041L }}</ref> and more recently by implicit (fixed-point) differentiation of the converged contraction equations, which avoids the memory overhead of unrolling the CTMRG iteration.<ref name="implicit-diff">{{cite journal |last1=Francuz |first1=A. |last2=Schuch |first2=N. |last3=Vanhecke |first3=B. |title=Stable and efficient differentiation of tensor network algorithms |journal=Physical Review Research |volume=7 |article-number=013237 |year=2025 |issue=1 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevResearch.7.013237 |arxiv=2311.11894 |bibcode=2025PhRvR...7a3237F }}</ref> Gradient-based optimization also enabled the accurate computation of excitation spectra of two-dimensional systems within PEPS.<ref name="peps-excitations">{{cite journal |last1=Vanderstraeten |first1=L. |last2=Haegeman |first2=J. |last3=Verstraete |first3=F. |title=Simulating excitation spectra with projected entangled-pair states |journal=Physical Review B |volume=99 |article-number=165121 |year=2019 |issue=16 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.99.165121 |arxiv=1809.06747 |bibcode=2019PhRvB..99p5121V }}</ref> Alternative strategies include variational Monte Carlo sampling of PEPS,<ref name="wang-vmc">{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=L. |last2=Pižorn |first2=I. |last3=Verstraete |first3=F. |title=Monte Carlo simulation with tensor network states |journal=Physical Review B |volume=83 |article-number=134421 |year=2011 |issue=13 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.83.134421 |arxiv=1010.5450 |bibcode=2011PhRvB..83m4421W }}</ref><ref name="liu-vmc">{{cite journal |last1=Liu |first1=W.-Y. |last2=Du |first2=S.-J. |last3=Peng |first3=R. |last4=Gray |first4=J. |last5=Chan |first5=G. K.-L. |title=Tensor network computations that capture strict variationality, volume law behavior, and the efficient representation of neural network states |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=133 |article-number=260404 |year=2024 |issue=26 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.133.260404 |pmid=39879037 |arxiv=2405.03797 |bibcode=2024PhRvL.133z0404L }}</ref> isometric tensor network states,<ref name="isotns">{{cite journal |last1=Zaletel |first1=M. P. |last2=Pollmann |first2=F. |title=Isometric tensor network states in two dimensions |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=124 |article-number=037201 |year=2020 |issue=3 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.124.037201 |pmid=32031848 |arxiv=1902.05100 |bibcode=2020PhRvL.124c7201Z }}</ref> and — less well controlled but highly scalable — contraction schemes based on [[belief propagation]].<ref name="bp">{{cite journal |last1=Tindall |first1=J. |last2=Fishman |first2=M. |title=Gauging tensor networks with belief propagation |journal=SciPost Physics |volume=15 |article-number=222 |year=2023 |issue=6 |doi=10.21468/SciPostPhys.15.6.222 |doi-access=free |arxiv=2306.17837 |bibcode=2023ScPP...15..222T }}</ref>
=== Tensor network renormalization ===
A very active line of research concerns real-space renormalization group algorithms that coarse-grain a two-dimensional tensor network — a partition function of a classical lattice model, or the norm of a PEPS — by locally truncating and recombining its tensors. The tensor renormalization group (TRG) introduced the basic coarse-graining step based on singular value decompositions,<ref name="trg">{{cite journal |last1=Levin |first1=M. |last2=Nave |first2=C. P. |title=Tensor renormalization group approach to two-dimensional classical lattice models |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=99 |article-number=120601 |year=2007 |issue=12 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.99.120601 |pmid=17930489 |arxiv=cond-mat/0611687 |bibcode=2007PhRvL..99l0601L }}</ref> and was extended to a unified framework for symmetry-breaking and topological phase transitions.<ref name="terg">{{cite journal |last1=Gu |first1=Z.-C. |last2=Levin |first2=M. |last3=Wen |first3=X.-G. |title=Tensor-entanglement renormalization group approach as a unified method for symmetry breaking and topological phase transitions |journal=Physical Review B |volume=78 |article-number=205116 |year=2008 |issue=20 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.78.205116 |arxiv=0807.2010 |bibcode=2008PhRvB..78t5116G }}</ref> The truncations were improved by taking the environment of a tensor into account (second renormalization, SRG),<ref name="srg">{{cite journal |last1=Xie |first1=Z. Y. |last2=Jiang |first2=H. C. |last3=Chen |first3=Q. N. |last4=Weng |first4=Z. Y. |last5=Xiang |first5=T. |title=Second renormalization of tensor-network states |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=103 |article-number=160601 |year=2009 |issue=16 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.103.160601 |pmid=19905683 |arxiv=0809.0182 |bibcode=2009PhRvL.103p0601X }}</ref> and the higher-order singular value decomposition version (HOTRG) made the approach applicable to three-dimensional classical and two-dimensional quantum systems.<ref name="hotrg">{{cite journal |last1=Xie |first1=Z. Y. |last2=Chen |first2=J. |last3=Qin |first3=M. P. |last4=Zhu |first4=J. W. |last5=Yang |first5=L. P. |last6=Xiang |first6=T. |title=Coarse-graining renormalization by higher-order singular value decomposition |journal=Physical Review B |volume=86 |article-number=045139 |year=2012 |issue=4 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.86.045139 |arxiv=1201.1144 |bibcode=2012PhRvB..86d5139X }}</ref>

A conceptual shortcoming of plain TRG is that it fails to remove short-range entanglement at criticality, so that it does not produce a proper renormalization group flow with the correct fixed points.
