This was first addressed by an entanglement-filtering scheme — which also provided one of the earliest routes to symmetry-protected topological order<ref name="gu-wen-tefr">{{cite journal |last1=Gu |first1=Z.-C. |last2=Wen |first2=X.-G. |title=Tensor-entanglement-filtering renormalization approach and symmetry-protected topological order |journal=Physical Review B |volume=80 |article-number=155131 |year=2009 |issue=15 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.80.155131 |arxiv=0903.1069 |bibcode=2009PhRvB..80o5131G }}</ref> — and solved systematically by tensor network renormalization (TNR), which inserts disentanglers in the coarse-graining step,<ref name="tnr">{{cite journal |last1=Evenbly |first1=G. |last2=Vidal |first2=G. |title=Tensor network renormalization |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=115 |article-number=180405 |year=2015 |issue=18 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.115.180405 |pmid=26565444 |arxiv=1412.0732 |bibcode=2015PhRvL.115r0405E }}</ref> and which was shown to generate the multiscale entanglement renormalization ansatz.<ref name="tnr-mera">{{cite journal |last1=Evenbly |first1=G. |last2=Vidal |first2=G. |title=Tensor network renormalization yields the multiscale entanglement renormalization ansatz |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=115 |article-number=200401 |year=2015 |issue=20 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.115.200401 |pmid=26613421 |arxiv=1502.05385 |bibcode=2015PhRvL.115t0401E }}</ref> Alternative formulations include loop optimization (loop-TNR),<ref name="loop-tnr">{{cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=S. |last2=Gu |first2=Z.-C. |last3=Wen |first3=X.-G. |title=Loop optimization for tensor network renormalization |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=118 |article-number=110504 |year=2017 |issue=11 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.118.110504 |pmid=28368642 |arxiv=1512.04938 |bibcode=2017PhRvL.118k0504Y }}</ref> graph-independent local truncations (GILT),<ref name="gilt">{{cite journal |last1=Hauru |first1=M. |last2=Delcamp |first2=C. |last3=Mizera |first3=S. |title=Renormalization of tensor networks using graph-independent local truncations |journal=Physical Review B |volume=97 |article-number=045111 |year=2018 |issue=4 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.97.045111 |arxiv=1709.07460 |bibcode=2018PhRvB..97d5111H }}</ref> and the manifestly positive TNR+ scheme, which generates explicit renormalization group flows in the space of Hamiltonians, making direct contact with Kadanoff's spin blocking.<ref name="tnr-plus">{{cite journal |last1=Bal |first1=M. |last2=Mariën |first2=M. |last3=Haegeman |first3=J. |last4=Verstraete |first4=F. |title=Renormalization group flows of Hamiltonians using tensor networks |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=118 |article-number=250602 |year=2017 |issue=25 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.118.250602 |pmid=28696763 |arxiv=1703.00365 |bibcode=2017PhRvL.118y0602B }}</ref> At criticality these methods give direct numerical access to fixed-point tensors and to conformal data (central charge and scaling dimensions), and the approach has grown into a field of its own with applications ranging from three- and four-dimensional statistical mechanics to lattice field theory and quantum computing.<ref name="meurice">{{cite journal |last1=Meurice |first1=Y. |last2=Sakai |first2=R. |last3=Unmuth-Yockey |first3=J. |title=Tensor lattice field theory for renormalization and quantum computing |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |volume=94 |article-number=025005 |year=2022 |issue=2 |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.94.025005 |arxiv=2010.06539 |bibcode=2022RvMP...94b5005M }}</ref>

=== Contraction of arbitrary tensor networks ===
For tensor networks without a regular lattice structure — as arise in quantum circuit simulation, counting problems and probabilistic inference — the cost of contraction is governed by graph-theoretic properties of the network, in particular its [[treewidth]].<ref name="markov-shi">{{cite journal |last1=Markov |first1=I. L. |last2=Shi |first2=Y. |title=Simulating quantum computation by contracting tensor networks |journal=SIAM Journal on Computing |volume=38 |pages=963–981 |year=2008 |issue=3 |doi=10.1137/050644756 |arxiv=quant-ph/0511069}}</ref> Efficient algorithms for identifying optimal or near-optimal contraction sequences have been developed,<ref name="pfeifer">{{cite journal |last1=Pfeifer |first1=R. N. C. |last2=Haegeman |first2=J. |last3=Verstraete |first3=F. |title=Faster identification of optimal contraction sequences for tensor networks |journal=Physical Review E |volume=90 |article-number=033315 |year=2014 |issue=3 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.90.033315 |pmid=25314572 |arxiv=1304.6112 |bibcode=2014PhRvE..90c3315P }}</ref> and hyper-optimized contraction planners based on hypergraph partitioning brought orders-of-magnitude further speedups.<ref name="gray-kourtis">{{cite journal |last1=Gray |first1=J. |last2=Kourtis |first2=S. |title=Hyper-optimized tensor network contraction |journal=Quantum |volume=5 |article-number=410 |year=2021 |doi=10.22331/q-2021-03-15-410 |doi-access=free |arxiv=2002.01935 |bibcode=2021Quant...5..410G }}</ref> These techniques underpin the classical simulations of random quantum circuits, and these works have progressively closed the gap claimed by quantum supremacy experiments,<ref name="huang-sycamore">{{cite arXiv |last1=Huang |first1=C. |display-authors=etal |title=Classical simulation of quantum supremacy circuits |year=2020 |class=quant-ph |eprint=2005.06787}}</ref><ref name="liu-sc21" /><ref name="pan-bigbatch" /><ref name="pan-sampling" /> as well as the tensor network simulations of IBM's error-mitigated dynamics experiments.<ref name="tindall-ibm" /><ref name="begusic" />

=== Finite entanglement scaling ===
At a quantum critical point the entanglement entropy diverges logarithmically, so no finite bond dimension MPS can represent the state exactly. Rather than a shortcoming, the finite bond dimension acts as a controlled infrared cutoff, analogous to a finite system size: it induces a finite correlation length, and critical properties can be extracted by scaling in the bond dimension (or in the induced correlation length), in direct analogy with [[finite-size scaling]]. The first such scaling analysis appeared in the corner-transfer-matrix context,<ref name="nishino-fes">{{cite journal |last1=Nishino |first1=T. |last2=Okunishi |first2=K. |last3=Kikuchi |first3=M. |title=Numerical renormalization group at criticality |journal=Physics Letters A |volume=213 |pages=69–72 |year=1996 |issue=1–2 |doi=10.1016/0375-9601(96)00128-4 |arxiv=cond-mat/9601078 |bibcode=1996PhLA..213...69N }}</ref> the scaling of MPS entanglement at criticality was subsequently quantified,<ref name="tagliacozzo">{{cite journal |last1=Tagliacozzo |first1=L. |last2=de Oliveira |first2=T. R. |last3=Iblisdir |first3=S. |last4=Latorre |first4=J. I. |title=Scaling of entanglement support for matrix product states |journal=Physical Review B |volume=78 |article-number=024410 |year=2008 |issue=2 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.78.024410 |arxiv=0712.1976 |bibcode=2008PhRvB..78b4410T }}</ref> a theory of finite-entanglement scaling was formulated,<ref name="pollmann-fes">{{cite journal |last1=Pollmann |first1=F. |last2=Mukerjee |first2=S. |last3=Turner |first3=A. M. |last4=Moore |first4=J. E. |title=Theory of finite-entanglement scaling at one-dimensional quantum critical points |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=102 |article-number=255701 |year=2009 |issue=25 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.102.255701 |pmid=19659096 |arxiv=0812.2903 |bibcode=2009PhRvL.102y5701P }}</ref> the interplay of finite-size and finite-entanglement effects was analyzed,<ref name="pirvu-fes">{{cite journal |last1=Pirvu |first1=B. |last2=Vidal |first2=G. |last3=Verstraete |first3=F. |last4=Tagliacozzo |first4=L. |title=Matrix product states for critical spin chains: Finite-size versus finite-entanglement scaling |journal=Physical Review B |volume=86 |article-number=075117 |year=2012 |issue=7 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.86.075117 |arxiv=1204.3934 |bibcode=2012PhRvB..86g5117P }}</ref> and a systematic scaling hypothesis unifying these approaches was put forward.<ref name="vanhecke-fes">{{cite journal |last1=Vanhecke |first1=B. |last2=Haegeman |first2=J. |last3=Van Acoleyen |first3=K. |last4=Vanderstraeten |first4=L. |last5=Verstraete |first5=F. |title=Scaling hypothesis for matrix product states |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=123 |article-number=250604 |year=2019 |issue=25 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.123.250604 |pmid=31922783 |arxiv=1907.08603 |bibcode=2019PhRvL.123y0604V }}</ref>

The same philosophy applies to PEPS in two dimensions, where finite correlation length scaling in iPEPS was established independently by two groups,<ref name="corboz-fcls">{{cite journal |last1=Corboz |first1=P. |last2=Czarnik |first2=P. |last3=Kapteijns |first3=G. |last4=Tagliacozzo |first4=L. |title=Finite correlation length scaling with infinite projected entangled-pair states |journal=Physical Review X |volume=8 |article-number=031031 |year=2018 |issue=3 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevX.8.031031 |arxiv=1803.08445 |bibcode=2018PhRvX...8c1031C }}</ref><ref name="rader-lauchli">{{cite journal |last1=Rader |first1=M. |last2=Läuchli |first2=A. M. |title=Finite correlation length scaling in Lorentz-invariant gapless iPEPS wave functions |journal=Physical Review X |volume=8 |article-number=031030 |year=2018 |issue=3 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevX.8.031030 |arxiv=1803.08566 |bibcode=2018PhRvX...8c1030R }}</ref> and extended to a full scaling hypothesis for PEPS.<ref name="vanhecke-peps">{{cite journal |last1=Vanhecke |first1=B. |last2=Hasik |first2=J. |last3=Verstraete |first3=F. |last4=Vanderstraeten |first4=L. |title=Scaling hypothesis for projected entangled-pair states |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=129 |article-number=200601 |year=2022 |issue=20 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.129.200601 |pmid=36461996 |arxiv=2102.03143 |bibcode=2022PhRvL.129t0601V }}</ref>
== Theory ==

=== Approximability and area laws ===
The mathematical justification for tensor network methods rests on approximability theorems. Early insight came from the study of the spectra of Baxter's corner transfer matrices: for integrable models these spectra — which are precisely the entanglement spectra probed by DMRG truncations — decay exponentially, explaining the remarkable accuracy of DMRG with small bond dimensions.<ref name="peschel">{{cite journal |last1=Peschel |first1=I. |last2=Kaulke |first2=M. |last3=Legeza |first3=Ö. |title=Density-matrix spectra for integrable models |journal=Annalen der Physik |volume=8 |pages=153–164 |year=1999 |issue=2 |doi=10.1002/andp.19995110203 |arxiv=cond-mat/9810174}}</ref><ref name="okunishi-ctm">{{cite journal |last1=Okunishi |first1=K. |last2=Hieida |first2=Y. |last3=Akutsu |first3=Y. |title=Universal asymptotic eigenvalue distribution of density matrices and corner transfer matrices in the thermodynamic limit |journal=Physical Review E |volume=59 |pages=R6227–R6230 |year=1999 |issue=6 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.59.R6227 |pmid=11969725 |arxiv=cond-mat/9810239 |bibcode=1999PhRvE..59.6227O }}</ref> The general statements are the proof that ground states of gapped local one-dimensional Hamiltonians satisfy such area laws,<ref name="hastings" /> together with the faithfulness theorem — states whose Rényi entropies obey suitable area laws are efficiently approximated by MPS.<ref name="faithfully" /><ref name="schuch-entropy" /> Together these results establish that DMRG operates in a provably adequate variational class. Building on these structural insights, an algorithm has been constructed that provably finds the ground state of any gapped one-dimensional local Hamiltonian in polynomial time — even if the algorithm itself is not very practical.<ref name="lvv">{{cite journal |last1=Landau |first1=Z. |last2=Vazirani |first2=U. |last3=Vidick |first3=T. |title=A polynomial time algorithm for the ground state of one-dimensional gapped local Hamiltonians |journal=Nature Physics |volume=11 |pages=566–569 |year=2015 |issue=7 |doi=10.1038/nphys3345 |arxiv=1307.5143 |bibcode=2015NatPh..11..566L }}</ref> Area laws in higher dimensions and their relation to simulability are still open problems.<ref name="eisert">{{cite journal |last1=Eisert |first1=J. |last2=Cramer |first2=M. |last3=Plenio |first3=M. B. |title=Colloquium: Area laws for the entanglement entropy |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |volume=82 |pages=277–306 |year=2010 |issue=1 |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.82.277 |arxiv=0808.3773 |bibcode=2010RvMP...82..277E }}</ref>

=== Canonical forms and the fundamental theorem of MPS ===
The map from tensors to states is not injective: different tensors can generate the same state. The canonical form of matrix product states fixes this gauge freedom,<ref name="pgvwc">{{cite journal |last1=Pérez-García |first1=D. |last2=Verstraete |first2=F. |last3=Wolf |first3=M. M. |last4=Cirac |first4=J. I. |title=Matrix product state representations |journal=Quantum Information and Computation |volume=7 |pages=401–430 |year=2007 |issue=5&6 |doi=10.26421/QIC7.5-6-1 |arxiv=quant-ph/0608197}}</ref> and the ''fundamental theorem of matrix product states'' asserts that any two tensors generating the same state are related by a local gauge transformation.<ref name="pg-string" /><ref name="cirac-mpdo">{{cite journal |last1=Cirac |first1=J. I. |last2=Pérez-García |first2=D. |last3=Schuch |first3=N. |last4=Verstraete |first4=F. |title=Matrix product density operators: Renormalization fixed points and boundary theories |journal=Annals of Physics |volume=378 |pages=100–149 |year=2017 |doi=10.1016/j.aop.2016.12.030 |arxiv=1606.00608 |bibcode=2017AnPhy.378..100C }}</ref><ref name="molnar">{{cite journal |last1=Molnar |first1=A. |last2=Garre-Rubio |first2=J. |last3=Pérez-García |first3=D. |last4=Schuch |first4=N. |last5=Cirac |first5=J. I. |title=Normal projected entangled pair states generating the same state |journal=New Journal of Physics |volume=20 |pages=113017 |year=2018 |issue=11 |doi=10.1088/1367-2630/aae9fa |arxiv=1804.04964 |bibcode=2018NJPh...20k3017M }}</ref> This theorem underlies much of the structural theory of tensor networks. When a state is invariant under a physical symmetry, the theorem forces the symmetry to act on the virtual indices through (possibly projective) representations; this explains string order,<ref name="pg-string">{{cite journal |last1=Pérez-García |first1=D. |last2=Wolf |first2=M. M. |last3=Sanz |first3=M. |last4=Verstraete |first4=F. |last5=Cirac |first5=J. I. |title=String order and symmetries in quantum spin lattices |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=100 |article-number=167202 |year=2008 |issue=16 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.100.167202 |pmid=18518239 |arxiv=0802.0447 |bibcode=2008PhRvL.100p7202P }}</ref> the degeneracies in entanglement spectra of topological phases,<ref name="pollmann-es">{{cite journal |last1=Pollmann |first1=F. |last2=Turner |first2=A. M. |last3=Berg |first3=E. |last4=Oshikawa |first4=M. |title=Entanglement spectrum of a topological phase in one dimension |journal=Physical Review B |volume=81 |article-number=064439 |year=2010 |issue=6 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.81.064439 |arxiv=0910.1811 |bibcode=2010PhRvB..81f4439P }}</ref> and it underlies the complete classification of [[Symmetry-protected topological order|symmetry-protected topological]] (SPT) phases in one dimension, obtained independently by several groups.<ref name="chen-gu-wen">{{cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=X. |last2=Gu |first2=Z.-C. |last3=Wen |first3=X.-G. |title=Classification of gapped symmetric phases in one-dimensional spin systems |journal=Physical Review B |volume=83 |article-number=035107 |year=2011 |issue=3 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.83.035107 |arxiv=1008.3745 |bibcode=2011PhRvB..83c5107C }}</ref><ref name="schuch-spt">{{cite journal |last1=Schuch |first1=N. |last2=Pérez-García |first2=D. |last3=Cirac |first3=I. |title=Classifying quantum phases using matrix product states and projected entangled pair states |journal=Physical Review B |volume=84 |article-number=165139 |year=2011 |issue=16 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.84.165139 |arxiv=1010.3732 |bibcode=2011PhRvB..84p5139S }}</ref><ref name="pollmann-spt">{{cite journal |last1=Pollmann |first1=F. |last2=Berg |first2=E. |last3=Turner |first3=A. M. |last4=Oshikawa |first4=M. |title=Symmetry protection of topological phases in one-dimensional quantum spin systems |journal=Physical Review B |volume=85 |article-number=075125 |year=2012 |issue=7 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.85.075125 |arxiv=0909.4059 |bibcode=2012PhRvB..85g5125P }}</ref>

=== Parent Hamiltonians and gaps ===
Every injective MPS is the unique ground state of a frustration-free, local, gapped ''parent Hamiltonian'' — the central result of the original papers on finitely correlated states.<ref name="fnw-cmp" /> This construction reverses the usual logic of many-body physics: instead of solving a given Hamiltonian, one starts from a state with prescribed entanglement structure and builds Hamiltonians for which it is exact, the AKLT model being the paradigmatic example.<ref name="aklt-cmp" /> These results establish that the manifold of injective MPS is in one to one correspondence with ground states of gapped quantum spin chains.<ref name="rmp" />

=== PEPS, topological order and bulk–boundary correspondence ===
For PEPS the virtual degrees of freedom acquire a richer role. A bulk–boundary correspondence has been established in which the entanglement spectrum of a region is described by a boundary Hamiltonian acting on the virtual indices along its edge — providing an explicit lattice realization of the [[Entanglement spectrum|entanglement Hamiltonian]].<ref name="cirac-poilblanc">{{cite journal |last1=Cirac |first1=J. I. |last2=Poilblanc |first2=D. |last3=Schuch |first3=N. |last4=Verstraete |first4=F. |title=Entanglement spectrum and boundary theories with projected entangled-pair states |journal=Physical Review B |volume=83 |article-number=245134 |year=2011 |issue=24 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.83.245134 |arxiv=1103.3427 |bibcode=2011PhRvB..83x5134C }}</ref> [[Topological order]] manifests itself in PEPS not through any local order parameter but as a purely ''virtual symmetry'' of the local tensor: this has been formalized through the concept of G-injectivity, which yields topological ground-space degeneracy and anyonic excitations,<ref name="g-inj">{{cite journal |last1=Schuch |first1=N. |last2=Cirac |first2=I. |last3=Pérez-García |first3=D. |title=PEPS as ground states: Degeneracy and topology |journal=Annals of Physics |volume=325 |pages=2153–2192 |year=2010 |issue=10 |doi=10.1016/j.aop.2010.05.008 |arxiv=1001.3807 |bibcode=2010AnPhy.325.2153S }}</ref> and the generalization to matrix product operator (MPO) algebras — MPO-injectivity — captures all models in the same phase as string-nets and provides explicit tensor network representations of anyon fusion and braiding.<ref name="sahinoglu">{{cite journal |last1=Şahinoğlu |first1=M. B. |last2=Williamson |first2=D. |last3=Bultinck |first3=N. |last4=Mariën |first4=M. |last5=Haegeman |first5=J. |last6=Schuch |first6=N. |last7=Verstraete |first7=F. |title=Characterizing topological order with matrix product operators |journal=Annales Henri Poincaré |volume=22 |pages=563–592 |year=2021 |issue=2 |doi=10.1007/s00023-020-00992-4 |arxiv=1409.2150 |bibcode=2021AnHP...22..563S }}</ref><ref name="mpo-inj">{{cite journal |last1=Bultinck |first1=N. |last2=Mariën |first2=M. |last3=Williamson |first3=D. J. |last4=Şahinoğlu |first4=M. B. |last5=Haegeman |first5=J. |last6=Verstraete |first6=F. |title=Anyons and matrix product operator algebras |journal=Annals of Physics |volume=378 |pages=183–233 |year=2017 |doi=10.1016/j.aop.2017.01.004 |arxiv=1511.08090 |bibcode=2017AnPhy.378..183B }}</ref> The anyonic excitations of such phases appear in the tensor network as "shadows" — topological information carried by the virtual level that cannot be detected by any local operator.<ref name="shadows">{{cite journal |last1=Haegeman |first1=J. |last2=Zauner |first2=V. |last3=Schuch |first3=N. |last4=Verstraete |first4=F. |title=Shadows of anyons and the entanglement structure of topological phases |journal=Nature Communications |volume=6 |article-number=8284 |year=2015 |doi=10.1038/ncomms9284  |doi-access=free|pmid=26440783 |pmc=4600714 |arxiv=1410.5443 |bibcode=2015NatCo...6.8284H }}</ref> The same MPO algebras underlie the tensor network formulation of the ''strange correlator'': overlapping a topological PEPS with a site-factorized product state — a diagnostic originally introduced for symmetry-protected phases<ref name="you-strange">{{cite journal |last1=You |first1=Y.-Z. |last2=Bi |first2=Z. |last3=Rasmussen |first3=A. |last4=Slagle |first4=K. |last5=Xu |first5=C. |title=Wave function and strange correlator of short-range entangled states |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=112 |article-number=247202 |year=2014 |issue=24 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.112.247202 |pmid=24996105 |arxiv=1312.0626 |bibcode=2014PhRvL.112x7202Y }}</ref> — produces the partition function of a critical two-dimensional statistical model whose non-local topological symmetries are exactly the MPO algebra of the original state, thereby giving an explicit lattice mapping from topological to conformal field theories.<ref name="vanhove-strange">{{cite journal |last1=Vanhove |first1=R. |last2=Bal |first2=M. |last3=Williamson |first3=D. J. |last4=Bultinck |first4=N. |last5=Haegeman |first5=J. |last6=Verstraete |first6=F. |title=Mapping topological to conformal field theories through strange correlators |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=121 |article-number=177203 |year=2018 |issue=17 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.121.177203 |pmid=30411961 |arxiv=1801.05959 |bibcode=2018PhRvL.121q7203V }}</ref> A gauging map promotes global symmetries of tensor network states to local gauge symmetries at the level of the tensors, connecting SPT phases, topological phases and lattice gauge theories within a single constructive framework.<ref name="gauging">{{cite journal |last1=Haegeman |first1=J. |last2=Van Acoleyen |first2=K. |last3=Schuch |first3=N. |last4=Cirac |first4=J. I. |last5=Verstraete |first5=F. |title=Gauging quantum states: From global to local symmetries in many-body systems |journal=Physical Review X |volume=5 |article-number=011024 |year=2015 |issue=1 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevX.5.011024 |arxiv=1407.1025 |bibcode=2015PhRvX...5a1024H }}</ref>

The algebras formed by matrix product operators have emerged as the natural lattice incarnation of generalized (categorical, non-invertible) symmetries. It has been shown that all dualities of one-dimensional quantum lattice models — including Kramers–Wannier, Jordan–Wigner and Kennedy–Tasaki transformations — are implemented by MPO intertwiners classified by (bi)module categories.<ref name="lootens-prxq">{{cite journal |last1=Lootens |first1=L. |last2=Delcamp |first2=C. |last3=Ortiz |first3=G. |last4=Verstraete |first4=F. |title=Dualities in one-dimensional quantum lattice models: Symmetric Hamiltonians and matrix product operator intertwiners |journal=PRX Quantum |volume=4 |article-number=020357 |year=2023 |issue=2 |doi=10.1103/PRXQuantum.4.020357 |arxiv=2112.09091 |bibcode=2023PRXQ....4b0357L }}</ref> Building on this, it was shown that every gapped phase of a one-dimensional system is dual to a symmetry-broken phase, that entanglement spectrum degeneracies are induced by the duality MPOs, and that simulating an optimally chosen dual model can substantially reduce the entanglement — and hence the cost — of DMRG simulations, placing symmetry-breaking, SPT and topological phases within a "generalized Landau paradigm".<ref name="lootens-natphys">{{cite journal |last1=Lootens |first1=L. |last2=Delcamp |first2=C. |last3=Verstraete |first3=F. |title=Entanglement and the density matrix renormalization group in the generalized Landau paradigm |journal=Nature Physics |volume=21 |pages=1657–1663 |year=2025 |issue=10 |doi=10.1038/s41567-025-02961-2 |pmid=41098545 |pmc=12518129 |arxiv=2408.06334 |bibcode=2025NatPh..21.1657L }}</ref>

== Applications beyond quantum many-body physics ==
Tensor networks are also used as low-rank representations in numerical multilinear algebra and scientific computing. In computational fluid dynamics, tensor-train and matrix-product-state representations have been used to compress and simulate turbulent flows and to represent high-dimensional turbulence probability distributions.<ref name="gourianov-turbulence" /><ref name="gourianov-pdf" /> In numerical analysis, tensor cross interpolation (TCI) constructs tensor-train or matrix-product-state representations by adaptively sampling selected entries of a high-dimensional tensor, with applications including multidimensional integration, partial differential equations, partition functions and matrix product operators.<ref name="tci" /> In classical statistical mechanics, partition functions and transfer matrices can be represented as tensor networks and evaluated or coarse-grained using methods such as CTMRG and tensor renormalization.<ref name="ctmrg" /><ref name="trg" />

Tensor network contraction is an important approach for classically simulating quantum circuits, as described above.<ref name="markov-shi" /><ref name="pan-sampling" /> In [[machine learning]], MPS/tensor-train models are used for supervised learning and generative modelling,<ref name="stoudenmire-schwab">{{cite conference |last1=Stoudenmire |first1=E. M. |last2=Schwab |first2=D. J. |title=Supervised learning with tensor networks |conference=Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 29 (NIPS 2016) |pages=4799–4807 |year=2016 |arxiv=1605.05775}}</ref> and tensor decompositions are an established tool for dimensionality reduction and large-scale optimization in data analysis.<ref name="cichocki" /> Through an exact duality with probabilistic graphical models, tensor networks also provide a language for classical probabilistic inference.<ref name="robeva-seigal">{{cite journal |last1=Robeva |first1=E. |last2=Seigal |first2=A. |title=Duality of graphical models and tensor networks |journal=Information and Inference: A Journal of the IMA |volume=8 |issue=2 |pages=273–288 |year=2019 |doi=10.1093/imaiai/iay009 |arxiv=1710.01437}}</ref> Tensor networks are used to decode [[quantum error correction|quantum error-correcting codes]],<ref name="ferris-poulin">{{cite journal |last1=Ferris |first1=A. J. |last2=Poulin |first2=D. |title=Tensor networks and quantum error correction |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=113 |article-number=030501 |year=2014 |issue=3 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.113.030501 |pmid=25083621 |arxiv=1312.4578 |bibcode=2014PhRvL.113c0501F }}</ref> and in high-energy theory the observation that MERA realizes a discrete version of [[Holographic principle|holography]] — with holographic quantum error-correcting codes as exactly solvable toy models of [[AdS/CFT correspondence|AdS/CFT]] — has motivated extensive use of tensor-network ideas in quantum gravity.<ref name="swingle">{{cite journal |last1=Swingle |first1=B. |title=Entanglement renormalization and holography |journal=Physical Review D |volume=86 |article-number=065007 |year=2012 |issue=6 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.86.065007 |arxiv=0905.1317 |bibcode=2012PhRvD..86f5007S }}</ref><ref name="happy">{{cite journal |last1=Pastawski |first1=F. |last2=Yoshida |first2=B. |last3=Harlow |first3=D. |last4=Preskill |first4=J. |title=Holographic quantum error-correcting codes: Toy models for the bulk/boundary correspondence |journal=Journal of High Energy Physics |volume=2015 |issue=6 |pages=149 |year=2015 |doi=10.1007/JHEP06(2015)149 |arxiv=1503.06237 |bibcode=2015JHEP...06..149P }}</ref> In computational condensed matter physics, tensor network methods (DMRG and PEPS) set benchmark results for paradigmatic strongly correlated models such as the two-dimensional [[Hubbard model]].<ref name="zheng">{{cite journal |last1=Zheng |first1=B.-X. |last2=Chung |first2=C.-M. |last3=Corboz |first3=P. |last4=Ehlers |first4=G. |last5=Qin |first5=M.-P. |last6=Noack |first6=R. M. |last7=Shi |first7=H. |last8=White |first8=S. R. |last9=Zhang |first9=S. |last10=Chan |first10=G. K.-L. |title=Stripe order in the underdoped region of the two-dimensional Hubbard model |journal=Science |volume=358 |pages=1155–1160 |year=2017 |issue=6367 |doi=10.1126/science.aam7127 |pmid=29191901 |arxiv=1701.00054 |bibcode=2017Sci...358.1155Z }}</ref>

== Limitations ==
Tensor network methods do not evade the exponential complexity of generic quantum states and high-dimensional tensors.

* '''Bond-dimension growth.''' Generic states, and even physical states outside the area-law regime, may require exponentially large bond dimensions. In real-time quantum dynamics the linear growth of entanglement translates into an exponential growth of the required bond dimension, which limits simulations to moderate times.<ref name="dmrg30" /><ref name="schollwoeck2011" />
* '''Contraction complexity.''' Networks with large [[treewidth]] generate exponentially large intermediate tensors, and the exact contraction of a generic PEPS is [[Sharp-P|#P-complete]].<ref name="markov-shi" /><ref name="peps-complexity" />
* '''Optimization.''' The variational objectives are non-convex; local-update methods can converge slowly or get trapped in metastable solutions, so careful convergence checks in the bond dimension, environment dimension and initialization are required.<ref name="schollwoeck2011" /><ref name="grad-corboz" />
* '''Approximation control.''' Truncations based on the singular value decomposition carry a local discarded-weight measure, but the accumulated error of repeated truncations, and of approximate two-dimensional contractions, does not in general admit simple rigorous global bounds.<ref name="schollwoeck2011" /><ref name="peps-complexity" />
* '''Dependence on representation.''' The computational cost depends strongly on the site ordering, the graph geometry, the implementation of symmetries and the gauge of the tensors, so that reported performance can vary substantially between implementations.<ref name="schollwoeck2011" /><ref name="chan" />

== Open-source software ==
A rich ecosystem of open-source tensor network libraries is actively maintained. Prominent examples include [[ITensor]], with C++ and Julia versions;<ref name="itensor">{{cite journal |last1=Fishman |first1=M. |last2=White |first2=S. R. |last3=Stoudenmire |first3=E. M. |title=The ITensor Software Library for Tensor Network Calculations |journal=SciPost Physics Codebases |volume=4 |year=2022 |article-number=4 |doi=10.21468/SciPostPhysCodeb.4 |doi-access=free |arxiv=2007.14822}}</ref> TeNPy, a Python library;<ref name="tenpy">{{cite journal |last1=Hauschild |first1=J. |last2=Pollmann |first2=F. |title=Efficient numerical simulations with tensor networks: Tensor Network Python (TeNPy) |journal=SciPost Physics Lecture Notes |volume=5 |year=2018 |article-number=5 |doi=10.21468/SciPostPhysLectNotes.5 |doi-access=free |arxiv=1805.00055}}</ref> the Julia ecosystem built on TensorKit.jl, with MPSKit.jl for matrix product state algorithms and PEPSKit.jl for two-dimensional simulations;<ref name="tensorkit">{{cite arXiv |last1=Devos |first1=L. |last2=Haegeman |first2=J. |title=TensorKit.jl: A Julia package for large-scale tensor computations, with a hint of category theory |year=2025 |class=cs.MS |eprint=2508.10076}}</ref><ref name="pepskit">{{cite arXiv |last1=Brehmer |first1=P. |last2=Burgelman |first2=L. |last3=Yue |first3=Z.-Y. |last4=Fedorovich |first4=G. |last5=Haegeman |first5=J. |last6=Devos |first6=L. |title=PEPSKit.jl: A Julia package for projected entangled-pair state simulations |year=2026 |class=cond-mat.str-el |eprint=2605.19960}}</ref> quimb, a Python library oriented towards arbitrary-geometry contraction and quantum circuit simulation;<ref name="quimb">{{cite journal |last1=Gray |first1=J. |title=quimb: A python package for quantum information and many-body calculations |journal=Journal of Open Source Software |volume=3 |issue=29 |pages=819 |year=2018 |doi=10.21105/joss.00819 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2018JOSS....3..819G }}</ref> and YASTN for tensor networks with Abelian symmetries.<ref name="yastn">{{cite journal |last1=Rams |first1=M. M. |last2=Wójtowicz |first2=G. |last3=Sinha |first3=A. |last4=Hasik |first4=J. |title=YASTN: Yet another symmetric tensor networks; A Python library for Abelian symmetric tensor network calculations |journal=SciPost Physics Codebases |volume=52 |year=2025 |article-number=52 |doi=10.21468/SciPostPhysCodeb.52 |doi-access=free |arxiv=2405.12196}}</ref>
